utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is in open session. I would like our Registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Thursday, January 15th, 2009, and I would like to welcome the representatives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj, and all the people in this courtroom. Mr. Seselj, I think I understood that you had a few housekeeping matters to deal with. If it's brief, you will have the floor. If you believe it's a bit longer, maybe it would be best to deal with this after the witness. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be very brief. It's just one housekeeping matter. Last night, I received a public document with confidential Annex B, the Prosecutor's request for the statement of Witness 1008 be admitted on the basis of Rule 92 quater. A few days ago, I received a similar submission from the Prosecution for another witness, so I don't want to make a written submission and waste your time, and I don't have that much time myself. I just wanted to express my disagreement and refer to Rule 6 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, where it says changes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] " ... an amendment shall enter into force seven days after the date of issue of an official Tribunal document containing the amendment, but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or other convicted or acquitted person, any pending case." Each case has three phases, pre-trial, trial, and appeal phases, and this is all pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 26th of February, when I first appeared in the courtroom, from 2003, nothing can be applied that is prejudicial to me, so the provisions of 92 quater cannot be applied if it's to my prejudice. Evidently, this is to my prejudice. And we're not talking about just these witnesses, but also witnesses who interfered in the affairs of God and picked their own time of death. In their own -- in any case, this Rule cannot be applied, and on the basis of Rule 6, I oppose that. And I cited an even more precise Rule a year ago of the ICC Rome Statute that has to do with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a quick oral reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. Seselj, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Of course, there is no prejudice to the rights of the accused by way of either 92 quater or 92 ter, those Rules, At least with respect to 92 ter, permit for cross-examination, but with respect to 92 quater, we've set forth in our application evidence that corroborates the evidence of the 92 quater witness, so we would submit there is no prejudice to the rights of the accused under those circumstances. And, of course, the Trial Chamber can give whatever weight they would deem necessary or worth those statements in light of all the evidence the Trial Chamber has heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber will rule on this later on. We'll rule on these pending motions. There are four, if I can remember, right? Maybe five. I've read them. I've noted that all these people had passed away, and that because of this, Rule 92 quater could very well apply. Now, regarding the legal merits of this and the debate, I mean, you've already mentioned this, and you've already raised this. The Appeals Chamber said that the amendments to the Rule could be applied retroactively. Now, the problem is to know where the prejudice might be, if there is a prejudice. There might be a prejudice if you are totally unable to challenge the content of such statements, but of course you can make a written submission to challenge the said declarations, explaining that the deceased witness said something, but since you're challenging this on -- according to such and such documents, you must back what you're saying. And then also when you call your own witnesses, if you do have witnesses, or if you do testify, you can come back to this, saying, Mr. X, who passed away, said this or that, and I believe that it was a lie, or this or that, and you can just challenge it. Just imagine the following assumption: Let's say that such a document could be essential to prove the innocence of an accused. That would mean that justice would not take it into account. Or assume that it would be absolutely essential to prove the guilt of someone, and then justice would turn a blind eye to it? No, that's a real problem. This debate has already been -- has already occurred. You've already raised the issue a number of times. It's the entire problem of retroactive application of amendments to the Rules. Here we have decided on a certain method and principle, and that's the way it is. You've just made an oral submission. If your associates and yourself can challenge, in writing, the statement, saying that the witness said such and such on such and such paragraph, but this is not backed by anything, or you can counter it, do it, because, remember, this is a mixed [indiscernible], there is both written submissions and oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you said that these statements can also prove the innocence of an accused. Of course, if we are proving the innocence of an accused, then it can be accepted, because it's not prejudicial to the accused. No civilised legal order would permit the retroactive application of criminal or criminal procedural law if it's detrimental to the accused. I did hear of such an interpretation by the Appeals Chamber, but it's quite primitive and unprofessional, and is not suitable for any civilised national legal system. And it's up to me to express my opposition, but you will do what you wish. I've seen that you're already working in that sense. You accepted the statement of Ljubisa Petkovic, even though it cannot be pursuant to Rule 92 quater, because it refers to written statements and transcripts provided by a person that has, in the meantime, deceased. Ljubisa Petkovic is not deceased. Thank God for that. He's healthy and well and a deputy in the Serbian Assembly. Or a person who cannot, in due diligence -- but as far as Ljubisa Petkovic here -- is concerned here, he was brought before you and he was sentenced, but he didn't even want to appear, or a person who is not physically or mentally fit, but his status such that he is physically and mentally fit, but he doesn't wish to testify, you were not able to apply this particular Rule to him. Yesterday, you were surprised when I said that I have a lot of objections to the work of the Trial Chamber. This is one of the major objections, and in my closing statement, I'm going to list all the other major objections that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Seselj. Your objection is now on the transcript. As far as the Article 92 quater, you're right, it has to do with deceased persons, but not just deceased persons; also, people who cannot be found and other persons who are ill, who are in such poor physical condition that they cannot come and testify. That's the merits of Article 92 quater, deceased people and some others. But now we know what your position is, and we take into account what you say, even if sometimes you feel that we don't. Let's now bring the witness into the courtroom. Let me remind the Prosecution that it has one hour for examination-in-chief, Mr. Seselj, one hour. But it's true the Judges sometimes ask questions, so when we say an hour each, that usually means an entire hearing day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Could you please give us your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Zoran Stankovic. I was born on the 9th of November, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us what is your profession at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently, I'm a professor of forensic medicine at the Faculty of Dentistry in Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're a civilian, or are you in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a Major-General of the Army of Yugoslavia. At the moment, I am a professional military person who is retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, have you ever testified in court? And if so, in which court and in which case, regarding, of course, the events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before this Tribunal on two occasions. Once, I was present during the proceedings of General Krstic, and then in May I was an expert witness for the Defence in the trial of Milutinovic, Sainovic, Ojdanic, Pavkovic,and Lazarevic, and Lukic. As for other courts, I was summoned to testify before the Special Court in Belgrade in the Zvornik case, and then I testified about the killing of Serbs in Gospic before the Higher Court in Deakin in Croatia. And now, on several occasions, I worked with the main prosecutor -- the Chief Prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the matter of killings of Serbs in locations where I performed autopsies, such as Kravica, Zvornik, Batkovic, Rogatica, Bratunac, Milici and some other places, Srebrenica, also some other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you well regarding this Tribunal, you have testified twice as a Defence witness in Krstic and Milutinovic et al, and it is the first time you are testifying for the Prosecution; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. You have already testified in this Tribunal, so you know exactly how the procedure runs. I'll be very brief in my explanations, thus. Of course, today you are a Prosecution witness and not a Defence witness, but in my book it's pretty much the same thing, whether you are on one side or the other, when it comes to the procedure. You will be answering questions put to you by the OTP representative, Mr. Ferrara. I'm sure you've met him, and he will put questions to you and will probably show you a number of documents. The Trial Chamber has allotted one hour for this examination-in-chief. Of course, the Judges can step in at any moment, and I probably will, in order to put additional questions or follow-up questions on some aspects of the work you were doing at the time. Then after that phase, Mr. Seselj, the accused in these proceedings, who's on your left, will also put questions to you during his cross-examination. As you know, this is an adversarial procedure. First the Prosecution puts questions and then the Defence puts questions to the witness. In a nutshell, this is how the proceedings will occur. Please try to be very specific in your answers, but I'm not too worried about this. You're quite a seasoned witness, if I may say so. And if you don't understand a question, just ask the person putting the question to reformulate it. If at any moment you feel uneasy - even a physician can feel ill at ease or bad at one point in time - just raise your hand and ask for a break. So I will now immediately give the floor to Mr. Ferrara for his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to say something. It doesn't matter to me if I am a Defence or a Prosecution witness. I don't mind whose witness I am. I will do my best to state the truth in everything that I say, as I know it. So I don't see any difference in being a Defence witness or a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, good morning. Could you please tell us briefly about your background and occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the Faculty of Medicine in Nis. After that, I served my regular military term of duty. I completed the reserve officers school's medical section, and after that for a year I interned at the hospital in Nis, and then I was the chief of the medical service in the Pec Barracks. After a year and a half, I was proclaimed the best young doctor in the JNA, and I was sent for specialisation in forensic medicine, which I did at the VMA, where I passed this exam in 1980. After that, I stayed there to work as a forensic doctor. At the beginning of the war, I began to conduct autopsies of people who died in the conflict. I went to several locations. First, I was processing soldiers. After that, I went to Vukovar, where I was head of the medical team in the investigations conducted by the Military Court in Belgrade. Then I worked at mass graves of Serbs who were killed in Gospic, in the area of Siroka Kula, which was followed by two occasions of autopsies of Muslims killed in Zvornik. Then I worked on members of the VRS who were killed in Zvornik. Then I worked in Fakovici, Rogatica, Milici, Vlasenica. I went to Sarajevo also. I also worked in Banja Luka, at a mass grave in Mirkonjic Grad as well, I went to Brcko also, Ugljevik, Bijeljina, and then I was also in Herzegovina, close to Mostar in Bjelasnica, Nevesinje. Perhaps I skipped some locations, but I did all of these things with a team from the Military Medical Academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness. You have mentioned the autopsies that you have performed, but looking at your written statement, it mainly deals with Zvornik. Vukovar was not mentioned in that statement, but you've just talked about Vukovar, and I'm requested in this. I'm not going to ask you any questions on the autopsies performed regarding Vukovar, but you said something that could be of interest to Judges. You said, on line 9, page 9: "I went to Vukovar, where I was head of the medical team in the investigations conducted by the Military Court in Belgrade." This sentence that we have now on the transcript, and which reflects what you said, is quite interesting. Could you please tell us exactly when the Military Court in Belgrade commissioned you to perform these -- this investigation and the autopsies, if need be? So when were you commissioned, please, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] On the 19th of November, 1991, I was informed by the chief of the institute that I should go to Vukovar, where we would be exhuming the bodies of some soldiers and officers who were killed in a tank. I think that on the 20th of November, we were there for the first time in Vukovar. It was either the 20th or the 21st of November. After that, on our return from Vukovar, I received an order from the chief of the institute. He told me that the military judge had decided that we need to go to Vukovar. I think we were on the 21st of November in Vukovar. On the 21st of November, we continuously processed the bodies of those we found who were killed in the territory of Vukovar. I think that this was until the 17th or 18th of December there. After that, I came back to Belgrade with the team, and then on three or four more occasions, we went there to inspect the dead who were found in the demolished buildings or in the area of the Municipality of Vukovar. I think that this was after the new year in 1992. I recall going there twice. I cannot really give you the exact date without the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are saying, and it's quite important, that as early as November 1991, you were told to go to Vukovar to examine the bodies of some soldiers and officers who were killed in a tank. Was it a mission of -- was it of a general purpose, or was it really a mission -- just a one-shot mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first time that I was there, this was a tank crew, as I said, which was killed in a house. Among them, there was a soldier from Novi Sad, Zoran. Also, Sergeant Jovic was wounded. He was transferred to the Vukovar Hospital and then to Belgrade. This was pursuant to the orders of the Military Court which I carried out in that particular case. After that, we received an order and went as a whole team to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first time, the three, were they Serbs or Croats, the injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were soldiers who were members of the JNA. I am not able to tell you if they were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the first time you went there, you were commissioned to investigate what had happened to JNA soldiers. That was for the first time. Now, on the second time, could you tell us exactly what was your mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was our assignment to inspect all the bodies found in Vukovar and to make reports to document the autopsies conducted, and in particular to try to identify the bodies found. In that particular case, we had forms that we used in our work, and we used the same forms for all of our work in the war-afflicted area. There were four or five different types of forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I won't go into details, but on the second time -- I mean, I want to give the floor to Mr. Ferrara as quickly as possible. I want to finish with this topic first. The second time you were commissioned to examine the body of all people found in Vukovar, I have a technical question as far as this is concerned. Was your mandate to look at all bodies, Serbs and Croats alike, or only Serb bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It pertained to all the bodies, because we could not know whether they were Serbs or whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That is an important piece of information. All the bodies. And the second time you were given an order, was this an oral order or were you sent a written document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a written order on the investigations in Vukovar, and it was issued by the Court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, on the basis of a written order provided by the Military Court in Belgrade, you were asked to go to Vukovar to examine all the bodies of the people that had been killed. And now this is my last question and the most important one. On what date exactly did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That order was received, I think, on the 20th of November, 1991. But, by your leave, perhaps I have been speaking at great length, but may I say that this was a team consisting of investigating judges, headed by Judge Milomir Salic, and the investigation involved civilian judges from the territory of Vojvodina, Novi Sad, Apatin and the other courts that were close to Vukovar. Then there was the forensic team for on site investigations that was led by Mrakovic, who is deceased in the meantime, and they were involved in all the on-scene activities that were supposed to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we can no longer hear the speaker. Other microphones are on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... and criminal technicians in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, all microphones have to be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is important. As of the 20th November, 1991, the authorities, whether they be the military, the JNA, or the civilian authorities, by the presence of a number of judges, received an order whereby they were asked to examine all the bodies found in Vukovar. Does this mean that at that time, all the authorities wanted to shed light on the circumstances in which these people had died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. We also had monitors, checks from the International Community. Antonio Piler [phoen], a forensic expert from Spain, checked what I was doing, and he came on specific instructions from the UN, if I'm not mistaken, and he had insight into what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, that the monitors from the International Community, well, so be it. I wanted to know how the civilian and the military reacted in Serbia. This is something which we had no understanding of so far. Thanks to your presence here today, we have further information about this, and it is now on the transcript, as regards Vukovar, at any rate. We shall now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe there's a mistake in the transcript on line -- page 14, line 5, because I don't think you said "27 of September, 1991."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. 20th of November and not 27th. There is a mistake on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Stankovic, have you ever visited mass graves in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that I only visited them. I processed them with my team, the mass grave at the Jewish cemetery, the two mass graves that were at the Sloga stadium, and I don't know where else. As for everything that we found or that we learned were sites where victims were buried, we exhumed all of that, and then they were buried at the Bulgarian cemetery, if I'm not mistaken. There is voluminous documentation about this. And later on, the chairman of the Commission for Human Rights, Pavle Todorovic, ceded that to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a question. We thought you were going to testify about Zvornik, but what you're saying about Vukovar is interesting. Just one point of clarification. When you were in Vukovar, were you made aware of the fact that things had happened in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Vukovar, as I've already said, we processed all the bodies. As for the hospital, we visited the hospital, and in the immediate vicinity of the hospital, in a passage, we found buried corpses. I think there were about 50 of them, perhaps even more. And on the surface close to that area, there were another roughly 50 corpses that were right next to one another near the hospital. In the hospital, there were people -- there were wounded persons, and that is what we saw. As for what had happened in the hospital, we did not know about any details because at the moment when we started working, we were obsessed with our own work. Winter had started, it was extremely cold. The temperatures went down to even minus 20 centigrade, and we were in a hurry to get as many bodies as possible away from the surface of the ground because animals started attacking the bodies. Also, there were many dead animals around. All of this also involved a great deal of danger from land-mines, because practically all of Vukovar was covered with land-mines, so we sustained losses among our own people who were dealing with the corpses together with us. Actually, those who were our advanced team were victims. There were cases when the corpses themselves were mined, and we had to try to make due in different ways. First of all, we tried to move the corpses with some kind of ropes so that they wouldn't explode during the autopsies. It was terrible, all of this that we were doing there, and the conditions were very hard- THE COURT: Did you discover that more than 200 people from the Vukovar Hospital had disappeared or had been killed? Did you learn about that at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that moment, we didn't know. It was only later, when people started writing about this and talking about this. That's when I learned about it. Had we known that there were these bodies of these people who had been killed, we would have carried out the exhumation of their mortal remains, and we would have processed those bodies, too. At any rate, they would not have remained where they were and where they were found later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, you had no information that would lead you to believe that the people who were in the Vukovar Hospital had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you ever inspect the mass grave at Ovcara or Grabovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's continue with your personal background. You say that you are a Professor lecturing in forensic medicine. Where did you used to teach, where do you present your lectures?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I used to work as a professor of forensic medicine, not military forensic medicine, but forensic medicine from 1996 at the Police Academy in Belgrade and from two or three years ago at this privately owned Faculty of Dentistry in Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you give lectures abroad?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Twice, I was invited to lecture at Kings College in Cambridge. After that, I delivered a lecture at the British Parliament before the Foreign Relations Committee of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, then before the Parliament of the Ukraine. After that, I delivered a lecture about war victims in Paris. That is when I met Florence Hartmann. She attended that lecture in 1995. Then I attended in the Netherlands, the first team that we brought to The Hague Tribunal. The chief Prosecutor was Mr. Gullstone [phoen], and then this was a group of Serbian inmates from the Sarajevo and Dretelj camps and others, including a woman who had been raped in these camps, an old woman. After that, I delivered lectures in The Hague, Amsterdam, we were in Utrecht, and that would be about it. Perhaps I may have omitted something.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Have you written books or papers on the topic of the identification and exhumation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We did write, for instance, for this foundation called "Truth About the Serbs ." I wrote two books for them. One is "The Crime Awaits Punishment" and another one "A Crime is a Crime." Then a book "Genocide Against the Serbs" between 1991 and 1993, and after that there were some others. I don't need to refer to all of that. We made a few films about the suffering of Serbs and members of the army in the armed conflicts, and then "Murderers Come Wearing Masks." It speaks of people who were killed in Gospic. They were Serbs who were killed in Gospic in 1991. There were a few exhibitions that were organised as well, and so on and so forth, but there was quite a bit of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So you have mentioned all the experience that you have had dealing with mass or multiple graves during war situation. Can you explain us the peculiarities of examining the bodies in war areas?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a very special kind of work, in view of the way in which we, from the Military Medical Academy, did this. We were the only team in the area, that is to say, in the area of the former Yugoslavia, that conducted its activities during combat operations close to the very front-lines while the conflicts were still going on between the warring parties. Under such circumstances, we had certain limitations, which meant that we could not expect any kind of large-scale technical assistance, because as a rule, there was no electricity in the areas. These were remote places. Then I, as the head of the team, had to take care of the people that I worked with, so that people would not get killed or injured, because I was responsible for their safety and security too. Also, we were expelled, for instance, to work on external examinations of bodies, not autopsies. Sometimes, whenever possible, we tried to carry out partial autopsies when we could not define the source of the injury, whether it was a projectile or shrapnel. But in principle, all of these activities took place in wintertime, when our possibilities were extremely limited, since the dead bodies were frozen. So we could not carry out autopsies, and it was very difficult for us to take off the victims' clothes. However, what we did do, which is doctrine in such situations, is the following: First and foremost, we wanted to register the parts of bodies that we found; also, to take all the main identification information that would later assist in the identification of these persons. Then, depending on the scope of our possibilities, to state what the implements were that caused these injuries, to take off the clothing from the bodies, and then to dry the clothing, as we did in Vukovar, for instance. We did that at some kind of a brick factory or something, so that later on the relatives and families could try to identify the persons involved on the basis of their clothes. Then we also took personal belongings from the clothing and from the bodies themselves; for example, valuables that we packed in special plastic bags. And we left them on the sites where we had worked so that people could try to recognise their nearest and dearest on the basis of that. We had many problems, because some things had not been defined at all. For example, where do we leave these personal belongings, especially valuables? And then -- well, at any rate, it was a very special approach that was applied in these activities, and we did as much as we could do. After that, we compiled the so-called autopsy reports on the external examinations of the bodies, or partial autopsies, or anything we did and anything that we found while doing our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You were not asked to draft a report for this case; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I made a statement here, in the proceedings that were made at the request of the Prosecutor, as instructed by the Federal Government, and also in the proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic, but not in the proceedings against the accused Seselj present here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Concerning this statement you made to the Prosecution -- to the Prosecutor, in particular I'd like to direct your attention to the statement -- to your second statement given to the ICTY investigator on the 8th July 2003, and in particular to what happened in Zvornik. When were you asked to go to Zvornik for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The Military Court in Belgrade ordered us to report in Zvornik in order to examine dead bodies. I think that it was on the 29th of April for the first time, 29th of April, 1992. And then a team was set up. Actually, the head of the team was investigating judge Captain Mirko Stojanovic, and we took this mini bus to Zvornik together with him. That was the first time when we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are discussing an important point, I'd like to put a question to you. The military prosecutor in Belgrade, what was his name, who was it? If I'm putting this question to you, it is because I feel it is important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already mentioned, it wasn't the prosecutor, it was the military investigating judge, Captain Mirko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the military prosecutor at the time, what was he called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it was Papic. Perhaps it was Colonel Papic, but I cannot remember exactly who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm putting this question to you for the following reason: In the military code applied to the former Yugoslavia at the time, the investigating judge can come to a crime site and can carry out the investigation, but after that he submits his report to the prosecutor. The prosecutor can decide not to do anything about it, or can seize the military tribunal, or can ask another judge to continue with the investigation, so I would like to understand how the chain of responsibility worked as far as Zvornik is concerned, because we know, and this is something we will discuss again later, that there was a judge named Mirko Stojanovic, but this judge could not take decisions on his own about everything. So this is why I wanted to know who the acting military prosecutor was. According to you, this person was allegedly called "Papic." Mr. Ferrara, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So can -- can you tell us who were part of this team and what was the duty of each one, this team who went to Zvornik .

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, Mirko Stojanovic was head of the team. He was the head of the team, and he gave orders to carry out all the activities that were required to carry out the investigation. There was the crime technician team from the MUP of Belgrade, and they carried out their part of the job, and we were in charge of autopsies and external examinations of bodies that had been found and that were at the Alhos factory, at a machine department there, in plastic bags. Also, there were representatives of the public enterprise that was supposed to organise the funeral later on. They assisted us when we placed the bodies that we had processed into plastic bags. They were from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, this is a question for you. The OTP has had hundreds and thousands of witnesses. I don't have an exact figure, but I would like to know whether the OTP interviewed Mr. Mirko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I will check, Your Honour, and answer you later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will let me know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So, Dr. Stankovic, were you told the ethnicity of the bodies you were going to examine on the Alhos factory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When we came to the site, we were that told they were Muslims who had been found in a forest below Kula Grad in Zvornik. This is a locality, Kula Grad, I mean, that is above Zvornik, above the lake, and that is where there were armed clashes between the Serb forces and the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the Alhos factory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was some kind of a factory. I don't know what it was that they actually manufactured. When you'd cross the bridge from Mali Zvornik, when you enter Zvornik, you'd pass by Karakaj, and then on the right-hand side there was this factory, where the bodies had been brought. When we crossed the bridge, we were told to report at Alhos. On the first floor in Alhos, there was one room or two rooms where there were members of the police from Zvornik. That is where we reported. The investigating judge went to them, and then they said to us that behind the factory there was a room where there was machinery for heating, and right next to these heating machines there were plastic bags with the corpses of the Muslims that we processed. That is what these people had said, and that's what the investigating judge conveyed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know who collected these bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that these bodies were collected by the people who worked for the public company in Zvornik; that is to say, the governmental organs of Zvornik. The authorities then were Serbian, I think. I remember there was this municipality President called Grujic then. And as far as I know, they brought them there to that locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How did you mark these bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: We marked these bodies by the letter Z, meaning "Zvornik." Roman numeral I, meaning the first examination, and then the number of the actual body. As we would examine a body, we would give it a number. When we started marking them, our first number was Z-I-24, I think it was. Since they had told us that before that, 23 bodies that had been found had been buried, we were to start with number 24. So that is how we marked the bodies that we processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you describe how the examination of the bodies took place? Was it a technique of autopsy, or was it only an external examination of the corpse?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: We based our work on the request made by the investigating judge. And after the investigating judge spoke to the representatives of the authorities in Zvornik, agreement was reached to carry out external examinations of the bodies, to describe the bodies, and to take all the clothes off the bodies, and to register all possible injuries that had been sustained, and also to note whether there were any blood-stains or any other kind of stains on the clothing, then also to have anything that may have been in or on the clothes taken out, and then to give these reports to the police that would try to identify the bodies on the basis of that; also, to remove possible valuables and other objects from the bodies that may have been there. Then also, wherever possible, to take finger-prints from the bodies, whenever possible, in order to establish their identity later, perhaps; then also to take other parameters for identification, like dental status, which was done, indeed; after that, to register possible tattoos, scars, or characteristic details on the bodies. That was also done. Also, to carry out external examinations and to establish injuries on the bodies in this way. Afterwards, to take photographs of the bodies, that is to say, before the autopsy in clothing, and then after the clothing would be taken over [as interpreted], photographs would be taken of the bodies, including injuries and other characteristics; and afterwards, to compose reports on external examinations and providing a certain opinion that could be defended and that would be derived from the findings that were the result of our external examinations of the bodies involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two technical questions. I am asking these questions because I have quite some knowledge when it comes to this area of expertise. Did you collect the bullets that were in the bodies? Was it done or not? If so, did you place the bullets in the plastic bag under seal with an identification number, or did you just do a very basic external examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we did not perform autopsies, but performed external examinations of the corpses, and for that reason we were not able and we did not look for projectiles in the body, and we did not act in the manner that we applied in other -- on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second question, another technical question: If, on a body, there was an entry wound and an exit wound, and if, on the body, there were several entry wounds and exit wounds, did you use rods in order to reconstruct the trajectory of the bullet, because -- if, of course, if there's an -- if there was an entry and exit wound, or numerous entry and exit wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can see that from the autopsy reports or the report on the external examination, that we provided that for all the fire-arms wounds we worked out the channel of the wound. Whether we did it from the exit to the entry wound or the entry to the exit wound, but in any case, this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It seems that you were also accompanied by policemen from -- forensic police. Did they collect powder, traces of powder, in order to see whether the shots had been fired at close range or at immediate range? Did you also check that maybe by collecting traces of powder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not take gunpowder samples, because we suspected only one body of having a point-blank wound, and we assumed that it was a killing, so in that case we didn't do it. But I have to say that in my country, we didn't have the proper equipment to be able to determine if there were any gun-shot traces. We didn't have electronic scanning or an electronic microscope in order to be able to find fragments of gunpowder. We did it in a non-specific method, and it's a method, as you know yourself, which means finding the traces of nitrates and other chemicals that would be present. But this method is not very precise, and we were unable, in that brief period of time, to carry out all of those activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. We could spend hours on this, but I'll try to be brief and to the crux of the matter. Regarding these examinations, as far as non-identified bodies are concerned, where there were no documents or nothing, did you check -- did you do DNA checks, or did you at least think about possible DNA checks, and did you take DNA samples in order to investigate this later on; collect hair samples, for example, or nails, or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were familiar with the DNA method of identification, but in the area of the former Yugoslavia no one had a lab where we could perform these analyses. Only at the -- in late -- the late 1990s, international donors provided a lab in Tuzla with such equipment. At that point in time, it was our assignment only to do what we were able to do, and possibly to try to exhume the unidentified bodies at a later stage, which was when we were planning to take our samples for DNA analysis. We did this later, when it became certain that there was the possibility to analyse the DNA samples. This was done in Sarajevo. So we did that then, but this was already 1999 or 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Spaniard who was supervising and monitoring this was in Vukovar, right, not in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in Vukovar, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Spaniard. I assume that this was a well-known technique in Spain at the time, so didn't he tell you that he didn't have the equipment yet, but that it would be good to collect samples in order to proceed later on to DNA checks, but he'd not thought about this? Hadn't he thought about this, this Spaniard specialist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we knew about it. But as I said, taking the DNA sample was planned for later. I must tell you that to this day, the samples that were taken for DNA analysis have not been all analysed because there are no funds for that. So, for example, a large number of persons are still waiting to be identified, in view of the limited resources that were at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But it's not because you can't do anything at a specific moment, that you can't think that later on, after a few months or a few years, you can't proceed to do something, but let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you remember how many bodies you examined in this first visit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the first visit, we began from Z-I-24 to Z-I-52. So it's approximately 28 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you identify the ethnicity of these bodies, and how?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: We did not deal with that particular matter. This is under the jurisdiction of the investigative judge. But among these people, we did register the fact that a certain number of them did have documents, personal ID cards, passports, or some other documents with their first and last name, and we did say that in our report, which persons these were. After that, all of these people were circumcised, indicating that they were Muslims. Based on the clothing, it was also possible to conclude that because of the presence of some green articles of clothing, the number of clothing items, it could be concluded that they were Muslims. What we were able to state, we did so, but the other questions that had to do with identification were in the jurisdiction of the Court that had requested the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What were the main causes of death of these people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of the 28 bodies that we examined at that time, in one case we could not determine the cause of death because the external examination of the body did not show any injuries. In two cases -- actually, in one case there was a stab wound in the region of the left side of the chest. In one case, there was a cut on the right side of the neck and the right side of the face. In the other 25 cases, they were all fire-arm wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did you draft the autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The autopsy reports were made sometime before or after the conversation with The Hague Tribunal investigators, based on the notes and all the material that I compiled during the autopsies and the external examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we have one of these autopsy reports, the ones with the 65 ter number 1238, on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before taking a look at these autopsy reports, notably number 24, who is quite interesting. That was the first one that you examined, obviously. Before you actually processed the body and examined the bodies, did you or the investigating judge, or those who were with you, and you were quite a number of people there, did anyone wonder where the body had been found, who had found the body, and whether, when the body had been found, there was a weapon next to this body? Were these questions asked? I mean, I have conducted a number of investigations, and normally when you do your job properly, this is exactly what you're supposed to do. So were these three questions put and answered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this question was posed by the investigative judge, who conducted investigations in that sense, but this was not part of my area of work or expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have talked to a good number of forensic pathologists like you, so please think twice about what you're saying. In the framework of your own job, if you suddenly learn that a body was found with no weapons and lying next to this body, there could be suspicion as to the reason of death, the cause of death. On the other hand, if you are told that he had a rifle in his hand, that could lead you to thinking that it was a fighter, and so you could go into different directions regarding your examinations. If you were told that ten bodies were found in a specific place without any weapons lying next to them, you -- what could spring to mind is that they were executed. So this kind of information is absolutely essential for the person who's going to do either the brief examination of the body or the autopsy, because that could lead him into different directions, as far as his conclusions are concerned. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that it's my duty to say, on the basis of -- on the basis of the examination, what type of injuries or wounds are involved, what were the weapons that they were inflicted with, that I have to say the cause of death, is it a killing, a suicide, or an accidental death, and at then that point I need to make my report. From then on, where the body was found, was it executed or not. This is the next phase of forensic study, which can be done only once the investigative judge or the person conducting the investigation - it can also be a prosecutor, you are correct - gathers all the other information and then gives that information to the expert, who will then be able to complete the report of whether this was an execution or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you're under oath. You're here to tell the truth. You're not here to pass the buck, you know, so I'm asking you very technical questions, and I want a technical answer. The technical answer is the following: If you're going to conduct -- if you're going to perform an examination on a body or an autopsy, I absolutely want to know whether your professional reflex was to immediately ask those who might have collected the body or might have brought the body or ask the policeman next to you whether they had this kind of information in order for you to do your job as best as possible. As I told you earlier, if you're told that ten people were found in a room, ten bodies were found in a room at a specific time, with no weapons at all in the room, you could draw some inferences from this, you could suspect some things. So I'm not trying to blame you for anything, but I just want to know how you proceeded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we found these bodies at the Alhos factory, where they were brought. When we asked where were these bodies found, we were told, and I already said this, that they were found just below Kula Grad, in a wood, where there had been fighting. So that was the whole information that I had about that event. So I did all that was within my jurisdiction, and then the investigative judge carried on the investigation from there on. I did not interfere in his area of expertise, but I did make a report on all my own findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were told that the bodies were found in Kula Grad, where there had been fighting. But the military police were there as well as the investigating judge who was a captain. None of these tried to find additional information to find out whether they had been discovered in a bunker on the front-line with weapons in their hands, yes or no? All these questions were not put and were not even investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that these questions were not asked, and this is stated in each of these reports at the beginning. At the time when we were conducting the examinations of the bodies, fighting was still going on around us, so in such circumstances none of the investigative organs could go to the sites and to make the investigations that you are asking about here. So whether at some later stage the investigative judge did actually do these things, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara, you have ten minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you describe the main entries of this autopsy report? Can you describe the main entries of this autopsy report? How did you structure this autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the first page of the report, it says: "Mirsad Kuljancic," so this is the person that we found documents on, and we put that in quotation marks because that was not a sufficient proof of identity. We simply indicated that perhaps it is that person, because we couldn't have confirmation that that was his definite identity, because the bodies were in the initial stages of decomposition and on a large number of cases the surface of the bodies was covered with maggots. On page 2, it says who the autopsy team was by first and last name, and the function of each of these persons. Then the location of the examination is given; also the remark that the fighting between the opposing forces in the immediate vicinity made the work of the teams very difficult and forced us to adapt to the existing situation. Then we explained the procedure of the clothing that was removed and where it was placed later, and what happened with the personal items that were taken from the bodies and given to the investigative judge. In the external examination, we indicated the length of the body, also an estimate of the weight of the body, the external characteristics of the body. Then we described the hair, the eyeballs or the eye hollows, also the state of the teeth, what sort of dental work had been done, if there were any missing teeth. Then we described the wounds that we saw, the gun-shot wounds, in which case we would try to determine the entry and exit wounds and the wound channel. In some cases, if there were a number of projectiles, we were not able to determine -- as I said, we described the entry and exit wounds, the channel of the wound. Then we would state the state of the composition of the body, what was the content of the bodily cavities. After that, we would describe the clothing, whether we found anything in the clothing or whether we found anything on the body. We also described if the clothing was torn or ripped by a projectile, if it was soiled, and with what. After that, we provided our findings, our views of the cause of death, whether it was bleeding or the injury to important life functions. Then we would say if the death was caused by killing or some other cause. In cases where we could not establish that, the cause of death was "killing," or when we were not sure, we would say that we were suspecting that it was a death by killing. After that, we marked the photographs. We would place them together with the report of the protocol, and this would be the content of the abduction -- of the autopsy report. And this is the procedure we followed in all of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So we can say that all of the reports concerning the 29 bodies that you examined at Alhos factory in this first visit were drafted following the same template; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I listened to what you were saying, and I was also looking at the report of the 24, and obviously all the indications you mentioned are on the report. It is well done. But something seems to be missing. Why don't you determine at least approximately the day or time of -- well, the time of death, that would be too complicated, but at least the day of death, with maybe the flies and the maggots found? Wasn't that possible? Because you did say that maggots were found on the bodies, and everyone knows that depending on the kind of maggot, you can find -- or you can try to determine the date of death, at least approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know yourself that determining the cause of death on the basis of bodily changes like the appearance of maggots and other bodily indications, and that on the basis of those it's very difficult to determine the time of death. At the time when I handed in the reports, I did not actually deal with that. Only at a later phase, based on all the parameters that I had mentioned and all the visible changes on the body that you could see on the photographs, I was able to perhaps form some kind of opinion. But this is something that I could consider a failure, because at the time I did not have time to deal with each particular case in such detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: But what was the condition of the bodies? Were they in a state of putrefaction or not, or were they fresh?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies were in the initial phase of decomposition, and this is stated in almost all of the reports. And in the photographs, it was evident that they were in this initial phase of decomposition and that some changes to the skin had already occurred, in terms of change of colour and prominent subcutaneous blood vessels, appearance of maggots and some other parameters. For example, I explained that the eyeballs were also in the initial stages of decomposition, so it was difficult to determine the state of the eye and the eye cavities. So all the bodies were more or less in the initial stages of decomposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So in relation to what the Presiding Judge asked you, from this kind of data, can you tell us approximately the time of killing of these people? So it was six months earlier or fifteen days earlier? Of course, I know it is a rough indication that you can give us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can just give a rough indication, but I couldn't really give you a complete rough indication due to the fact that I don't have information about exactly where the bodies were found. If they were found in a wood or in some environment which was colder, with lower temperatures, if it was a humid environment, then the process of decomposition is slower, and all of this influences the determination of the time of death. So on the basis of this information, it would be difficult to give you a detailed opinion as part of my testimony now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you remember if the majority of these persons were killed by one shot or by multiple shot -- shoots?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies of the victims with such injuries did have a number of wounds from fire-arm projectiles, some of them fired from hand weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were you asked by the Military Court to determine the period of time when these people were killed or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, it's 10.00 a.m., and it's time for the break, our 20-minute break. According to my computations, you have about 20 minutes left. Let's have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Ferrara, one point of clarification for the Bench. The witness you quoted, you quoted that person as a fact witness, not as an expert witness. Can you clarify this for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: He's an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this person is an expert witness, where is the expert's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to Rule 94 bis, an expert can testify on a report or on a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue, Mr. Ferrara, is in which capacity did you call this expert, because as far as we know, he was not called under Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Now, let me check.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. For years, this witness has figured as an expert in these proceedings. I always refer to him as an expert, and on the basis of Rule 67, I made a submission to the OTP in relation to this witness as an expert. So invariably, this witness always figured as an expert here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question has been settled, since the Trial Chamber ruled on this on the 24th of November. The Trial Chamber ruled on so many matters, anyway. We stated this witness would testify as an expert witness, and this is pursuant to Rule 94 bis. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Concerning your request on Mirko Stojanovic, I tell you that the OTP has never interviewed this man. We don't have any statement from this Mirko Stojanovic. In relation to the autopsy reports drafted by Dr. Stankovic, I would like to tender into evidence all the 99 -- 29 autopsy reports drafted on this first visit in Zvornik. I can read the related 65 ter number or I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better for you to have all the reports tendered. You're not going to tender them one by one. You would like the 29 reports to be tendered into evidence; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Twenty-nine, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 29 reports. Let's give an exhibit number to those 29 reports, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the whole batch of these autopsy reports will be given Exhibit P704. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. As far as I know, the fate of exhibits depends on whether an expert report or expert statement will be admitted beforehand. This is the first time that we have an expert who appears with a statement given to the OTP that was written by the OTP in his name and that was read out to him loud. So far, we've had only expert reports. I think that first of all you should decide whether you are going to admit this statement that the OTP wrote up for him as his report, and then only the expert -- the exhibits along with this expert statement. Perhaps you may refuse to admit the expert's statement, and then you are left with these other exhibits. I hope that you are going to refuse to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, for the benefit of the public, Rule 94 bis, testimony of expert witnesses, it says the witness statement or the witness's report, called to testify by one of the parties, is disclosed to the other party within 34 days, which means that the Trial Chamber can, after the cross-examination, admit the statement or dismiss it. This will depend on the cross-examination. For the time being, we have admitted the technical exhibits, i.e., the 29 examinations of corpses. This can be admitted. The statement can be dismissed and so on and so forth, but this exhibit we have. There is no reason why we should challenge the examination of these bodies. This is in the case file, and we shall see whether we admit it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And, of course, I anticipate that I will ask to tender the statement made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, let's move to your second visit in Zvornik. When did it take place?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another objection. Well, since Rule 94 bis speaks about the statement, and here we have two statements, the question raised now is: Which one of these two statements is a candidate for being admitted into evidence? To the best of my understanding so far, it is only the witness statement from the 1st of October, 2003. Now, is it both statements or only one statement, and can both statements be admitted into evidence? If the Prosecutor is asking for both to be admitted into evidence, then the logical question is: Why did he not bring them together in good time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may well ask whether the Prosecution is going to ask to have both tendered into evidence. If that is the case, the Trial Chamber will see whether both can be admitted, whether one or the other can be admitted. We have noted what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask to tender into evidence only the second statement, because it's the one related to our indictment. The first statement, the one made on 2001, I think, is related to location that are not involved in our indictment, like Srebrenica and others, so I don't think it is necessary to tender this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it will be the second statement. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, when did it take place, your second visit in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The second time, I was instructed by the Military Court to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Ferrara, you are discussing the second visit. If you will allow me, I would like to get back to the 29 autopsy reports. I thought you were going to put the question, but you may have forgotten about it because of the break. I would like to get back to number 24. As the Prosecutor has not put the question to you, I must put it to you. In your conclusion on the causes of death, in this field we always try to know what the causes of death are. On number 24, on the last line, you say that the death was probably due to a murder. This is the conclusion, which means that the examination you conducted led you to believe that there was a murder or killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the investigating judge was informed of the fact that there had been a murder. What does he do then, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the investigating judge did after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were part of the JNA. You ended up as a general in the army. Therefore, you are high-ranking military, even though you are a physician. According to the rules of the JNA in such a situation, the military investigation judge is informed of the fact that there has been a murder, what must he do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, he carries out investigative activities, which mean that there should be an on-site investigation of the place where the body was found. In peacetime, it was compulsory for us forensic medical experts to go, and we were the professional associates of the judge, and we collected all objects that could clarify the cause of death, and all the circumstances involved. After that, there is a proper process of compiling forensic documentation, including registering and photographing all details found on the scene. Then statements are taken from witnesses who are present or who had some knowledge in relation to the matter concerned. And after that, he asks the forensic medicine expert present there to describe the position where the corpse was found in, and perhaps biological traces that were found on the surface, or surrounding objects that were found. Also, he asks the medical forensic expert to convey to him other possible observations that have to do with his line of work. Once that is over, then he instructs or orders that the body be transferred to a site where the autopsy is carried out. After that, he sends samples to certain laboratories, where analysis is carried out, depending on the kind of analysis that should be carried out. Then once all of that is gathered, he also asks for an autopsy report from the forensic expert, forensic medical expert. And when he collects all these facts in relation to the incident concerned, he hands it all over to the military prosecutor, and then the military prosecutor decides whether he is going to bring charges against a person or persons unknown, or he may ask for additional investigations, including forensic expertise, which means that on the basis of all the information contained in the case file, the expert states his views regarding matters that are of interest for the case concerned. After this expertise is carried out, the expert sends this back to the investigating judge. And after all these activities, an indictment is issued. In our country, these are proceedings before a trial chamber. Depending on the crime concerned, the composition of the trial chamber is decided upon. This same kind of trial takes place, so the representatives of the prosecution are there and also the representatives of the injured party, and also experts that give questions to defence attorneys and to the accused, but this is the procedure that is applied in our jurisdiction and jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have given us a very comprehensive answer. We don't need to add any comments to this. If I have understood you correctly, once you have prepared your autopsy reports, which you handed over to the investigating judge, given that the conclusions stated that there had been a murder, he should have seized the prosecutor. As far as you know, did he do this or didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he did do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You believe so. And why did the prosecutor not pursue the matter, so as to identify the perpetrators of the murder? You may not have an answer to this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, my activities are only within my own line of work. Any kind of interference with the organs of the judiciary or prosecutors' organs could be misinterpreted. Therefore, I only act within the scope of my own authority and responsibility, in accordance with my own line of work. I believed that those who are in charge should carry all of this out, and if this did not take place, then that person should explain why.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We could spend a lot of time on this, but I'm checking the clock. I believe the Prosecutor has 20 minutes left, and Mr. Seselj has an hour. When you were heard, and this is part of your second statement, by the three representatives of the OTP - I shall not quote any names, but there were three of them - no one or none of the investigators asked you this question: You prepared this autopsy report; what happened to it? They were not interested in asking you this kind of question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said that the investigators asked me, "Where is Mirko Stojanovic," whether I know how they can establish contact with him. This is contained in my statement. Mirko Stojanovic was a military judge in Ljubinje. After the state fell apart, he was transferred to the Military Court Belgrade. Soon after the war broke out and after these investigations were carried out by him, he retired. And since then, I never had any contact with him, and I don't know where he went and what he does.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. You said, Mr. President, that this expert made a statement to three persons. That pertains to the first statement. The second statement was given only to one person, a woman, I think, Rita Pradhan. I would like to direct your attention to yet another thing; that the 8th of July is the date of the interview, and it was only on the 1st of October, 2003, that the witness had the statement read back to him. This is the short statement that was taken for these particular proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to the second statement. We have a statement of the 14th, 15th, 16th, 17th, 18th, and 19th of August. There are three people that have interviewed you. In the 8th of July, 2003 statement, there is one woman that interviewed you, Rita Pradhan. Whether it be the three people or this woman - this is an additional question - seemingly you were asked where this judge was. I'm sure it was easy to find him, but nobody put a question to you concerning the prosecutor to see what the prosecutor might have done, as far as you remember, of course? I know this happened a long time ago. I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I believe not," is what he said. It's not on the transcript. You said, "I believe not"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So, Professor Stankovic, again, when does it take place, your second report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The second time was on the 5th of May, 1992, at the instructions of the Military Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Who was present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, the following persons were present. Well, actually, the investigating judge did not go with us. He just issued an order and stayed in Belgrade. Dr. Milo Savljevic went, who was a trainee, and two assistants, Drajkovic [phoen] and Sojicic [phoen], and I. That was the forensic medical team from the VMA that took a separate car. Then after that, the representatives of the MUP of Belgrade came. They carried out their own work, and inter alia it was their duty to take photographs of the bodies that we were processing. They found us -- or, rather, we found the representatives of the public company from Zvornik, the ones who helped us in carrying the dead bodies that we were examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where did you go to examine these bodies; again in the Alhos factory or in another location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The same location, the same location where we had worked the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where did these bodies come from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: They told us that the bodies were also from Kula Grad, from the forest. And the bodies had already been brought to Alhos, and they were in this machine room, where the machines for heating the factory were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: But these bodies were not there when you went the first time on the 30th April 1992; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992, the bodies were not there. These were bodies that were brought in subsequently after we had dealt with the first bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Were they Muslim or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, we were told that these were Muslims. The persons who brought these bodies said that these were Muslims who were killed in the armed conflict between the warring parties in the area below Kula Grad in Zvornik; that is to say, that they had found them in that forest when they searched the area at a later point in time, these representatives of the public company. They put them in the plastic bags, and they brought them there to the place where we examined them on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many bodies did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many bodies did you examine on this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the second occasion, from Z-I-53 to Z-I-114.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you draft autopsy reports following the same template showed for the first -- for the first group of bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not compile autopsy reports because the photographs that were taken on that occasion were not submitted to me by the persons who had done that, the representatives of the MUP.
