When I asked for the photographs, they told me that they had been submitted to the Court in Zvornik, which I found unclear. I asked why the Court in Zvornik, when it was the Court in Belgrade that had ordered the investigation, and then they said, "You can address the people in Zvornik." And they told me there that they did not have those photographs there and that the judge was not there, and to this day these photographs had not been submitted to me. And I didn't want to compile a report without photographs and without any kind of evidence, video material, photo material, concerning registering the situation or concerning the bodies that I examined and the findings that I made during the autopsy. I have all the paperwork, that is to say, all the sets of documents from these examinations, everything that was written up. However, I did not compile a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's a mysterious point I would like to clarify. When you came the second time, there were representatives of the MUP. Everybody knows. People who don't will discover this is part of the Ministry of the Interior. This has got nothing to do with the army, as at the time you were there, because you were part of the military. If there were MUP representatives, what did this mean in terms of the proceedings? Does this mean that the civilian authorities or the civilian prosecutor might have an interest in this? Why was the MUP there? Can you answer this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Military Court did not have the technical means or the personnel to meet all the requests at the beginning of the war in the area of the former Yugoslavia. So in the case of Vukovar, when they engaged civilian judges for specific activities in Vukovar, on this occasion two, they engaged personnel from the Belgrade MUP who did have the appropriate equipment and were able to perform those tests, and they were more experienced than the military experts for dactyloscopies, since this was something that they did on a daily basis, and it was a routine procedure in their work, compared to the army, who had a different situation in terms of the military personnel and the military formations. So these people were asked to come in and assist. The investigative judge asked them to come. He put this request to the official from the police, who then met our request and helped us in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... contributed in technical terms, but this was still placed under the authorities of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was under the jurisdiction of the Military Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So you have never seen these photos, the photos related to this second group of corpse?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened during the end of this second visit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're thinking of, specifically. There were many things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you remember if you were shot by somebody, and how it happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the autopsies, we would place the body in a plastic bag - excuse me - and we would return the clothing to the plastic bag next to the body, because we expected that the relatives would come to identify the bodies also by recognising perhaps the clothing. Since these were bodies that were in an advanced stage of decomposition, the whole bag was so full of worms, I had never seen -- even though I had done so many autopsies, had to perform autopsies on bodies that had so many worms. We extracted from the clothing certain personal items and objects, and we placed them in an area outside of the Alhos factory so that the documents would dry, so that we could later hand them over to the people who were supposed to continue the identification process, people from Zvornik. After one such case when we packed the bodies like that, a group of people appeared with beards and cockades and other insignia, and we had a quarrel. I wouldn't allow them to come to the place where we were performing the autopsies, because pursuant to the rules, there is no place there for people who are not officially supposed to be there and part of the official investigation. So there was this quarrel or fight. They had their own reasons, probably, why they wanted to come there. I complained to a policeman who was there on the first floor, and I told him that he should make sure these people leave and that the documents that I was supposed to pack into the plastic bags should be gathered together. I was supposed to hand these documents over to the police. At that point in time, one of those men from that group pointed his rifle at me. I don't know if he was under the influence of alcohol, or I don't know what was the matter with him. I didn't expect him to actually shoot. But somebody who was standing next to him pushed his arm, and at that point a burst of fire, some two or three bullets - I don't know how many - just passed next to my head. At that point, I felt very difficult. I had to be quiet, and the reason I had to be quiet was that we had difficulties finding people who wanted to do autopsies under these conditions. It was difficult. Only somebody who was not on the front-line or in conditions like that can ask for a legal procedure for the inspection of these bodies. This was a quite surreal situation. There was a lot of agitation and excitement. There were all these groups of people. They left. I packed those clothes, and I didn't tell this story. I kept it to myself. I didn't want my associates to know about it or the media. I just wanted to continue, without disruption, with this autopsy work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who shot at you, he was probably a member of the unit. Since you were an officer, you had a degree of authority, and you could have mentioned this to your superiors. Why had you rather remained silent about this, because this was a rank-and-file shooting of an officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... soldier. It was a member of the so-called paramilitary military formations. Secondly, in an area where there was combat going on, and I'm hearing this quite often in this trial and in other trials, where people say you could tell who was a member of this unit or that unit, but the only way to differentiate between these people was to tell apart the members of the army. They had their own characteristic insignia, and you were able to differentiate, but I didn't see these people among members of the so-called Arkan's units who had their own type of clothing, the way they dressed. Otherwise, you could not tell who belonged to which formation. They would introduce themselves as coming from here or there, but you couldn't really check any of that; at least not when I was working in that area. There was nobody I could complain to, when I didn't know to which particular unit that person belonged, why he belonged to that unit. It was just total confusion among the people who were in the army, who practically experienced this breakup in the same way that I did. I couldn't believe that the state would fall apart, the former SFRY, and it fell apart like a house of cards. All those declared values that for years were the guiding light disappeared over night. Everything collapsed like a house of cards, and the bulk of the soldiers went to the newly-created institutions or organisations in the former territory of Yugoslavia. There was no one I could have complained to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can agree with you. But in 1992, when you go to Zvornik for the second time, I assume that the JNA was there. There must have been a military in charge there who was responsible for the entire area, notwithstanding the fact that there were paramilitary formations present, or was it total chaos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was total chaos. I will tell you one thing. I will go back to Vukovar. When we came to Vukovar with a team of civilian investigative judges, note-takers, all the technicians, when we went to certain locations where there were bodies found, we were not secured by the army. We were guarded by some members of the so-called Territorial Defence of Vukovar. Who these people were, I don't actually know, but they did their best to protect us from the firing that was underway in Vukovar, to protect us from the land-mines that were all over Vukovar and things like that. But this was total chaos, because the army at that time was composed of members of different ethnicities, and already there was a lot of confusion. Slovenia had already broken off. Croatia was in the process of breaking away, and then it was the turn of Bosnia and Herzegovina to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you -- so you don't know which unit these men actually belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, and I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You cannot?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they wanted to go inside and see these bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you go to Zvornik again after this second visit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: After the second visit, I went to Zvornik on several occasions because we were conducting autopsies of Serbs and members of the Army of Republika Srpska who were found at Glodjanska Brda and in Zvornik and its environs, and I think this was a total of six or seven times that I went there; I think so. Perhaps it wasn't that many times. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a marginal question for the Trial Chamber. It's very important for the Trial Chamber. Earlier, we mentioned chaos. So according to you, could you tell us whether the official army in place, the JNA, was it able to order the paramilitary units or, to your knowledge, was it unable to do so? Take your time before answering, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that in that area, and not only in that area, total chaos reigned in terms of relationships and subordination. Already at the time, as you know, Bosnia had declared its independence. I think it was around that time, and there was already talk about how members of the JNA had no business in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the army was preparing to pull out. In that situation, no one could have a dominant role and command these units, especially not in a situation when the army pullout was being prepared. No one had the authority to order paramilitary units how to behave. Once some kind of cooperation was established, we did have cooperation. I'm talking about the Military Medical Academy and myself, in charge of the autopsy, we had good cooperation with the Serbian Radical Party and the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. They had a person, a very responsible, serious man, Vojvoda Zoran Drazilovic, who was in charge of the corpses of volunteers who were killed, and he made sure that all the volunteers who were killed in that area were brought to the VMA. All the bodies were autopsied according to all the rules and the procedures applied in these circumstances. After that, he was in charge of taking the bodies, bringing the relatives in, identification, and so on and so forth, but this was at a later stage when these relationships were consolidated. Until the point of time when the army left that area, I think the 19th of May was the dead-line for the army to pull out of the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory, the rule applied that all the army members should pull out from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember I went to Sarajevo, to Dobrovoljacka Street. There was some soldiers and officers killed there. I was in charge of processing those bodies. I went to Sarajevo. After that, we were not allowed to go to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina anymore. This was forbidden - I'm talking about members of the army - to perform the activities that we had been performing before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ferrara, can I just ask the witness to add one sentence to your last statement. Are we to assume that after the 19th of May, the members of the JNA were ordered not to enter into Bosnian territory anymore? Did this prohibition apply also to the volunteer units? Could they, even after the 19th of May, still operate within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received this order in the army, and I know that in my case, after the 19th, after the army pulled out from Bosnia and Herzegovina, could not go to that area, because a command was formed there under the command of, I think -- yes, it was General Mladic who succeeded General Kukanjac. So after that, we had this ban. As for the volunteers, I really couldn't say, because I don't know that much about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did you have this good cooperation with the SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The cooperation began in 1992-1993 and continued until the end of the war. This was a person, Zoran Drazilovic, who was in charge of the volunteers, and all the volunteers regardless of the area of the former Yugoslavia where they perished were taken to the VMA, and autopsies were performed, preparations for burial were made, and then they were transported to the locations where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When did you go for the third time in Zvornik? So you said to perform duties on Serb victims. When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: This happened on the 16th of February, 1993. I received a summons from the Court president in Zvornik, Vasa Eric, to come and to assist in the processing and identification of corpses that they had found or that should have been exhumed or were to be exhumed for the Glodjanska Brda area. At the time, I submitted a request, because I had asked to go to that area and to help those peoples, since Serbs were killed in Sijekovac and Milici, and no one wanted to go because this was an area where there were combat actions. And then people from that area asked me to come in and to complete this job. The medical administration, pursuant to my request, replied that I could go, but only as a volunteer, and that as a volunteer in that area, they bore no responsibility about what happened to me, and they had no obligations towards my family if anything happened to me. I agreed to that, I said, yes, I would still go. After that, I went to Zvornik on that basis, and I was -- I reported to General Pandurevic, and he told us we would be going to Glodjanska Brda, where mass graves of Serb soldiers and civilians were found who had been killed in that area, that we would be taken there by a bus and by cars, and that a large group of journalists would go with us. And I think on the 19th, we came to Zvornik, and then on the 19th we went to exhume the bodies, and this was at the Glodjanska Brda location.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Just the last question. Was there any difference between the procedure you followed when you examined mass -- the Muslim bodies and the procedure you followed when you examined this mass grave with Serbian bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: There were deviations in the sense that now we were able to conduct partial autopsies. There were conditions in Zvornik then, which was outside of the combat zone area. Fighting was some 20 or more kilometres further away, and this was when we were able to and we had time, for example, to prepare the wound channels to see if the wound was a projectile wound or as a result of some other instrument, or weapon, or object, and that was the only difference that was there in doing these autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have further questions, and I ask to tender into evidence the statement on the 8th of July, 2003. The 65 ter number of this statement is 7429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will rule after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, before I ask to amend the Prosecution 65 ter exhibit list, because the statement is not included in our exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, the second one. But I have a question first, a very important question for this witness. Generally speaking, when I ask questions, you know, there is always a point to them, but here there really is a specific point, and something you mentioned on your own volition. You actually said, when you were talking about Zoran Drazilovic and the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, if I understood correctly in the translation, you said the following: "When a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party was killed in combat, his body was brought back to the Military Academy where it was autopsied." Hearing this, the question immediately springs to my mind. I would like to know whether the volunteers were treated in the privileged fashion. Why wasn't there an autopsy automatically for all other fighters who had fallen? Why were they specifically treated differently? Can you answer, please .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will reply. First of all, we did the autopsies on all members of the army, regardless of whether they were members of the JNA or the VJ who were killed in the war-afflicted area. Where volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were found, they were brought in together with these members of the JNA or were in some other way brought to the Forensic Medicine Institute. Then we were supposed to hand the remains to the families. We didn't have orders from the military judges or the investigative judges to conduct these autopsies, because when the war began, I submitted the first reports on autopsies of JNA members to the Military Court, and these autopsy reports were returned to me with the remark that these are persons killed in the war and that the Military Court is not interested in such victims. This is what happened, that's how it was. After that, on my own initiative, I began, with a group of workers and doctors from the VMA, to process these bodies, and then we had to ask permission from the General Staff, which we did receive, since some people from the institute did not agree with that particular method of work or with that kind of work at all. So when we received the body, depending on the wound, the condition of the body, we had to, for example, remove all the clothing and to document in some way these victims of war, because we believed -- I believed I am taking responsibility upon myself that in some future date some people will ask for reports of the deaths of their own members or of their own relatives. So this is how we did this particular kind of work. They didn't have any privileged position. They were just well organised and took care of their people, and they brought them in for processing and burial in a decent manner. I must say that we also had about ten volunteers of Arkan's. They were also brought in to the VMA from the area where they were, and we processed the bodies. And after that, we handed the remains over to the families or to the people in charge of such matters from different parties. As the war continued and more and more victims of war were found, we kind of became a centre where commissions for humanitarian issues, after exchanges of these mortal remains, would bring in these bodies for processing, and these people were not privileged in any way. It was just a regular activity that we performed, with the agreement of those people who decided on that and who were authorised for such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. So they did not have a privileged treatment because they were a member of the Serbian Radical Party. But out of your answer, another question crops up. It might be even more important. If the volunteers of the SRS are autopsied at the Military Academy, just like other soldiers of the JNA are autopsied, does this mean that you, yourself, considered them as enjoying the status of military personnel, and that because of that, they were under the control and the authority of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. All I believed, and still believe, is that we need to perform autopsies of people from the lowest ranks - I'm thinking of the financial status - and from the highest rank in exactly the same way, so regardless of who I was processing. There was no difference in the autopsies from person to person, regardless of their status or origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you understood the gist of my question. I will reformulate it. It's an important question, so I'm being extremely careful when it comes to your answer. I absolutely want to be sure that you fully understand the question. This is my question: You are in the JNA, you're in the structure. The Military Academy, where you performed your talents as a forensic pathologist, is competent when it comes to soldiers who were killed in combat. You told us that the JNA soldiers who had been killed were brought to you, as well as volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party, and you even added that at one point in time some members of Arkan's units were brought to you. So you are -- you represent the military authority there, but does this mean that the military authority considered that those who had been killed, that the SRS volunteers were actually soldiers, had the status of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time, I held the rank of lieutenant-colonel. Perhaps this is a high rank in the army, but I was far from the administrative structures and the policies which at the time were in force in my country. Since I was at a too-low level in order to be able to ask about these things, and there was no need for me to consult anybody about why we were doing something and how we were doing it, it is a fact that these people, not only the members of the SRS, and it was not only two but some ten members of Arkan's units, and some other civilians, also, from various parts of combat areas, but it's true that the army processed those corpses, that they paid for the costs of burial of these bodies, and that they covered the costs of transport from the VMA to the destination. We had two people from the General Staff who worked on this. They worked really well on it. They maintained all the contacts, and we never had any problems with that. The only thing is that the army covered all of the burial costs for these people, including the coffin, the clothes, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll supplement my question with an assumption. Let's imagine I'm a Serb civilian with my wife and children, and I'm driving in my car next to combat areas. And let's say that my car explodes on a land-mine and my entire family is killed, but I'm a civilian. So I would like to know whether my body and the body of my family members will be brought to the VMA for an autopsy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there was a request from the family or any organ, we carried out these autopsies. For example, journalist Zoran Amidzic from Sabac and his team got killed in Bosnia as they were on a news mission. During the night, a request arrived to carry out an autopsy of those bodies. That was supposed to be done during the night, and I went to Sabac, and I carried out the autopsies so that the bodies could be buried the next morning. Then, for example, there were quite a few people whose mortal remains had been exhumed or found in areas outside Serbia. These bodily remains would be exhumed, packed in bags, and then they were brought to the VMA, where we carried out autopsies. Also, for example, there was cooperation between these humanitarian commissions to agree on the exchanges of bodies of persons who had lost their lives in a particular territory. Once the bodies were brought in, we carried out autopsies. That is to say that we did all sorts of work at anybody's request, basically. Perhaps that may seem strange, but we did not ask for any kind of financial compensation, we never raised the issue. We simply wanted to help people in these most difficult situations so they would find out whether these were the bodies of their nearest and dearest or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the conclusion is quite straightforward. The Military Academy, where autopsies were performed, autopsied everyone, either from the military or civilians. They were just autopsying at requests.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Upon request, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, the same goes for medical treatment. That is to say that the Military Medical Academy admitted and treated all persons from war-ravaged areas. They were all admitted, regardless of their status, and that was the general position. That's how we operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to this last question and thanks to your answer, we can infer that the army had a competence to perform these autopsies because of the context, because it was an armed conflict. You're talking about a war-afflicted area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the clock, and I'm quite worried. Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I will be very quick. Just a technical question. Concerning the 29 autopsy reports that were admitted with just one exhibit number, that is Exhibit P704, they are already up-loaded in e-court with 29 different 65 ter numbers, so I need to tell the 65 ter number so that we will have just one number or we need to change again our 65 ter exhibit list, so I have quickly read the 29 number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that Mr. Ferrara does this on Tuesday. Today, I would not like to give up part of my time for cross-examination for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll solve this immediately. The Judges did wonder about this earlier, and we thought it would be best to have a single number, but we can also have 29 numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this can be done outside the court, to have these 29 exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ferrara, you will ask Mr. Mundis how to -- what to do. He knows exactly how I usually work in another case. So just put your 29 documents with the 65 ter number, and then next to it you will put the numbers. I think we were at P704, that was the last one. And then you will give the list to the Registrar, and the Registrar next week will tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: We already [indiscernible] the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, perfect. Then next week, the Registrar will give us the numbers. But now I would like to proceed with the cross-examination. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stankovic, when my associates, sometime in September 2005, disclosed to the public that on the 29th of August of that same year, I had submitted, on the basis of Rule 67 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, my intention to present a special defence, and I submitted that to the OTP, and I challenged your expertise and credibility. On several occasions you made statements to different media that you were not a Prosecution witness in the case against me; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because at the request of the OTP, which I have here, dated the 20th of December, 2002, the Minister of Justice, Mr. Savo Parkovic, received a request calling me to deal with case IT-02-54-T, the Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic. The decision of the Government of Serbia, dated the 6th of February, 2003, and the Federal Government of the 31st of January, 2003, speaks of that. Nowhere in my statement did I mention you, or did I say a single word about you. That can be seen from my statements. I don't know you, either. I saw you only once, when a book was being promoted at the army centre. I think that you were Deputy Prime Minister at the time. I never made any statements with regard to you. I didn't quite understand this. Everybody was talking about this. Everybody was reading some kind of material that you had written up, and that is why I made these statements. So that is the case. I have the original documents here, and you will see that you were never mentioned, and no decision was ever made for me to take part in your trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you realise that you were never announced as an expert in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, at least to the best of my knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was told that I was supposed to testify in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. This is what I was told by a lawyer, Momir Ivetic was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that has nothing to do with The Hague OTP. You were preparing to testify as an expert witness of the Defence there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So let's just clarify that. You found it very embarrassing that your name was officially on the list of Prosecution witnesses in this case, and you didn't find that pleasant; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is primarily because in the Serbian public, it is a shame when someone appears as a Prosecution witness in proceedings in The Hague; objectively, that's the way it is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, objectively, that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to put very brief questions to you, and please give answers as brief as possible so that we use this time efficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the accused please be asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question could not have been put, but it was put, and you answered clearly. If I understand correctly, when a witness comes to testify before this Tribunal, it is shameful to come and testify here, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I did not say that it was a shameful thing. I said something different. I particularly noted that at the very beginning, as a witness or as an expert, I am duty-bound to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. That's what I said in the oath, too. However, there is this particular notoriety thing that is going about, especially in my setting, that I come here to accuse someone, that I'm a man who has accused someone or is accusing some persons, whereas I came here as a person who conducted autopsies of Muslims in Zvornik, who compiled reports, and I came here to defend those findings and reports. It is not shameful for me to come before this Tribunal. I said that it was actually something that was unpleasant for me because of the way in which witnesses or experts of the Prosecution are being depicted in the setting where I live and work. That is the case. However, had I been ashamed in any way to appear before this Court, I would have found a thousand ways and means of evading that. However, I feel this responsibility that I should act in accordance with the requests made by the persons who are in charge of these proceedings, and that is why I came. That is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In your country, sir, there are trials also, and the witnesses come to testify at the request of the Belgrade prosecutor or from other towns. But when the witnesses come and testify before your tribunals, do they have a problem, or do they say to themselves, "I have been called by the prosecutor, and I shall go and testify"? What difference is there between this Tribunal and the tribunal in Belgrade, from a witness's standpoint? If this is a delicate question, you may say, "I had rather not answer." You don't have to answer. You can only answer if you wish to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Judge, in our country, we are very dissatisfied with some of the judgements made by Trial Chambers in The Hague, some Trial Chambers. This primarily has to do with the acquittal of Nasir Oric, and I'm a living witness to that. If you look at my statement that is given and the descriptions of the wounds, and the ways in which these people were killed in Srebrenica and the surrounding villages by Nasir Oric's units, this is a shameful judgement, and I can say that, and I can prove that. When evidence was needed, I provided these reports, but not all of them, because it was stated then we are asking for those reports, but we don't want those other reports. That is the first matter. The second matter: As far as Ramush Haradinaj's judgement is concerned, I carried out the autopsy of a driver, an Albanian from the municipality in Pec who had been killed by those units, and that was registered and that was handed in. The representatives of the International Community were there, and nothing. I was there, and the President Of the Committee for Violations of Humanitarian Law. I talked to Sharif Basuni [phoen], Carsten Hoffman, Goldstone, Carla Del Ponte, Louise Arbour, lots of people, and we provided lots and lots of documents, and there were no proceedings before this Court. As far as Gospic is concerned, we provided the expert findings for 14 bodies, and I went to the Court in Rijeka and explained my findings, and the Court admitted that. However, it is illogical for The Hague Tribunal not to analyse the killing of 24 civilians from Gospic, most of them women and elderly men, and over 100 of them were thrown into pits in Velebit. And General Norac is now getting married and travelling around Croatia. At this mass grave, there were 181 bodies of civilians and soldiers that were killed in that area. That is where General Matijasevic got killed, too, commander of the 6th Guards Brigade from Croatia. That is to say, this is direct participation of one country on the territory of another country. I found 36 old men there who were over 60 years old with the gravest possible injuries. So that is the matter. That is the bitterness that the citizens of my country feel as far as this Tribunal is concerned. This man who is present here, who insulted me like no one ever insulted me in my life and who presented so many untruths about me, but he is being tried here only because of what he said. He is only being tried for verbal offences. That is the feeling of the general public in my country, and that is my feeling. So that's the bitterness that is felt in that environment, and that is how this is viewed. We are not opposed to having all criminals punished, and this is precisely evidence. Had the Military Court carried out the investigation in Vukovar, also in relation to the Muslims in Zvornik, there was an investigation, this is proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have provided us with a very comprehensive answer. I thank you for having provided us with a lengthy answer. Now, two comments I'd like to make. Crimes were committed, and at the time the Prosecutor needed to prosecute the offenders of these crimes with due diligence. After meeting at the United Nations headquarter, we need to prosecute these offences now. As far as acquittals are concerned, I have nothing to say about that, because the Judges have handed down their judgement. You know as well as I do that when it comes to criminal offences, before somebody is found guilty, the evidence has to be adduced. That is what is called presumption of innocence. All the evidence needs to be gathered for an offence to be proven. That is what the problem is all about. This may be difficult to understand when one does not have a legal background, but anyone with a legal background will understand what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: You have said what you had to say. That is fine. Mr. Seselj, please proceed, because I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to need all of one hour that you have given me, so perhaps we can give up on the break, or we can work for longer hours, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have your time. Before the break, we have 20 minutes. Then we will have the break, and then we still have an hour left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, please, let us just have brief questions and brief answers. Is it correct that the Serbian public, in a vast majority, believes that The Hague Tribunal is an illegal court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The professional public believes that it is an illegal court. There are differences in views, but the way in which it was established gives these people the right to speak of it as an illegal court. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have already put this question. You have already taken a stand. This is not a trial of the Tribunal. We need to check, during the cross-examination, what the witness has said during his -- in his statement. Do not exploit the presence of the witness to address other issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what you wish to hear, you did hear during the examination-in-chief, and in response to questions put by the Judges. Now I am examining the expert witness about his credibility, and my questions are conceived on that basis, and I'm entitled to that. I know full well what I think about The Hague Tribunal, and you know that full well. However, I'm asking this witness about his knowledge as to what the Serbian public believes, especially the lawyers and professionals in the Serbian public, and of course I'm going to ask him what he thinks about it. I have the right to do that. If you will forbid me to do that, then there is no point in any cross-examination. I am challenging his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only problem, Mr. Seselj, is that this is outside the scope of his expertise. He has come here at the request of the OTP to discuss the examination of bodies and post-mortem examinations. He has not come to talk about political issues. If you feel that, in terms of credibility, he has not told us the truth, so be it, but you cannot ask him what he thinks and what the public opinion thinks about this Tribunal, that you're going to shed some light on the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to put questions in the cross-examination this way because, as you said, it's completely irrelevant to asses the credibility of the witness on his political opinion or that kind of opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when I was questioning Anthony Oberschall, the first witness, who is allegedly a doctor of sociology, and before that he got a degree in physics, I put questions to him from the area of physics and mathematics, and you saw that he did not know what imaginary numbers were and what Abogada's [phoen] number is. I have the right to do that. Also, I have the right to put questions to this expert witness, who's a general and who was Minister of Defence. I have the right to ask him about these matters of principle and these essential matters, and then on the basis of his answers, I and you, and the Prosecutor, and the professional public, can draw conclusions on his credibility. I know that you find these questions unpleasant, and maybe you will find the answers even more unpleasant, but at the moment when you agreed to be Judges of this Court, you knew that you may come across such unpleasant things. And now you are using my time for no reason whatsoever, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let me remind you that I was the person who let the witness talk and let him express his views, and asked him how public opinion reacted. Let me remind you that I did not cut him short and that I let him put his views forward. Now, during cross-examination, let me remind you that this is not an unlimited right and that you can't address just anything under the sun, and you are now addressing the issue of the legality of this Tribunal. This is not a legal expert, neither in constitutional law or on any other law, for that matter. What I'm interested in is: Do you have anything in your cross-examination that could prove useful to that, on the basis of the events that took place in Vukovar and Zvornik? That is what we are interested in. Everything else are things which you have already mentioned. We know about that. So you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... well, any time I yield, Mr. President, I always get a major headache, and I always regret yielding to you. Well, let me tell you this sincerely. But I'm going to yield once again. I am not going to ask him any legal questions. Because he was a Minister of Defence and he's a general, he's a retired general now, once a general, always a general, I then have a question which is not of a legal nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you've just said something, Mr. Seselj, that I knew nothing about. You said that this gentleman was Defence minister. Were you Defence minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was a defence minister from the 24th of December, 2005, until the 15th of May, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since he was defence minister, he is able to answer a number of questions, but I had to be informed about this. I knew nothing about this, but whether these are military issues or that tie into his job when he was Minister of Defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, as a former defence minister, are you aware that almost the entire Serbian public believes this to be an extremely anti-Serb court, in view of the number of Serbs that are being tried here and the few Croats, Muslims and Albanians, also having in view the vast differences in the sentences, and also in view of how many notorious criminals were freed and they are not of Serb ethnicity? Well, the witness did answer questions from you about that. He did say how the Prosecutor behaved towards the evidence he offered, so I'm not going to allow the Prosecutor to spend any of -- or use up any of my time, and I'm going to use up every minute that I have been allotted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... any am following the view. I said I object to this kind of question that are completely not relevant. The witness is here like an expert witness in forensic medicine, not to tell us his opinion and the opinion of the public in Serbia about the ICTY, or this Trial Chamber, or the Prosecution. So this kind of question can really not be admitted in court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I give up this question as well? All right, I will let it pass. Let me continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, according to my information you were, in some form - I'm not able to define that - an expert consultant of The Hague Prosecutor's office for autopsies and identification of bodies of Muslim soldiers who -- or which were exhumed in connection with the liberation of Srebrenica in 1995, both those who were killed in fighting or those who were executed; were you in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was not in any capacity connected with those investigations, especially not on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were not contacted by the Prosecution in that matter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence did so in the case against General Krstic, but not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you provided your expert views only for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But in that way, you acquired information about certain scandalous occurrences in the process of the work of the forensic medicine specialists from the West who took part in that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In my findings that I provided to The Hague Tribunal Trial Chamber made quite significant objections to some experts who conducted the processing and exhumation of bodies in Srebrenica and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Did you notice that the general tendency of those international forensic medicine specialists is to treat all the bodies found of Muslim soldiers in and around Srebrenica as victims of execution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the crucial objections that I made in writing is the fact that from 2.082 remains that were exhumed at that time from and around Srebrenica, 2.870 deaths happened, and I disputed that. How can you have a larger number of deaths than the number of remains?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the judgement by this Tribunal in the case of General Radislav Krstic, it was said that the Serbian forces executed between 7.000 and 8.000 Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree that it is possible to speak about such numbers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In my testimony, I drew attention or I wrote that this is one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I don't think we have any indictment about the Srebrenica location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am probing the expert credibility -- the expert's professional and ethical credibility. Depending on my questions, I'm going to draw conclusions as to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What I wanted to say is this: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat your question, can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the objection made by the Prosecution, we have documents that have been admitted. These documents have been prepared by international pathologists regarding a number of victims. We have these documents, and the Defence is now challenging the work of these international forensic pathologists, and quotes the example of Srebrenica, which I'm discovering as we going along. So that's how it is. We are not trying the Srebrenica case here, but in this manner some of the findings of the international forensic pathologists are being challenged. We have admitted their documents. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the most recent numbers, when we're talking about Srebrenica-related exhumations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but as you said, I did make the objection, and this is the basic problem: If somebody claims that 7.000 to 8.000 people were killed, then they have to have that number of mortal remains. In case there are none, the rules indicate that one should state the number of remains found, that the rest should be recorded as missing, and there should be a chance that domestic or international institutions search for the rest of the victims. We have cases, in fact, that a name that is at the memorial centre next to Srebrenica is the name of a person who actually did report as being alive a year or two years before that, and these are the information that I kept pointing to, and relating to the information about Muslim victims. It's well known what has been found, what has not been found, which remains were found, which names are being recorded as still missing. This is the information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, are there still mass graves which have not been exhumed yet? Do you know about this, since you are an expert involved in these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the report that I looked at, I think it's a report of Professor Wright, it says that a number of graves that were located and marked and that do contain mortal remains of people, have still not been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Stankovic, that at the memorial centre in Bratunac, which is actually a cemetery of Muslim soldiers, many Muslims were buried who were killed in various ways from 1992 to 1995, before the liberation of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did read about this and also came across remarks that all Muslims were being buried there who -- that all Muslims are buried there who actually are -- fell in some other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So evidently the goal is to increase the number of the dead as much as possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot reply to that question, but the number does grow with the number of burials of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the number is growing instead of stating how these victims died in Srebrenica or in the breakthrough out of Srebrenica or in executions? I'm not disputing that there were executions. There were executions. I agree with that, and people were found with hands that were tied; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that in my report. There were 2.082 remains, and 367 were found with blindfold or ligatures on their legs or arms, and it's evident that these people were executed. In other bodies, we did find gun-shot wounds, on some we did not, and this was stated in the report, whether such injuries were found or not. I mean, it's a question of expertise, and this can be checked back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is one problem that appears there. Some bodies -- on some bodies, bullets were found.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the clothing of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that possible evidence that these people were killed by a bullet from a distance, because if you are killed by a rifle bullet, it would go clean through the body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said in my report that gun-shot wounds can occur during execution or during combat or due to self-inflicted injuries or in some other ways. I don't want to go into all of them. Therefore, I did say that in these 360 people, I think this is the number, they were executed for sure. The rest is something that has to be established based on examinations and investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you dealt with this question, are you aware that the bulk of Muslim soldiers, when withdrawing from Srebrenica, were killed in mutual conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: There was talk about that, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that a team of Finnish pathologists, led by Helena Ranta, who is explaining now how the US governor of the OSCE, a worker, ordered her in the way in which she should investigate in Racak, that she compiled the bodies of Muslims killed in mutual conflicts in the forest near the village of Kravica, and only in one location did they find them dispersed all over the ground, and this was 594 bodies. Do you know about that? Do you know that Helena Rant a was involved in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So you don't know about this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What's the relevance of these questions? I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm testing the expert witness's of the Prosecution credibility. The Prosecution brings their expert here, and then they wonder why I'm testing their credibility. This is not a witness of the Defence, so that my questions are irrelevant. This is a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer. I had, myself, asked a few questions to the witness regarding point-blank shots and close shots, because this had not been mentioned in any of these 29 reports, because whether you're firing, you know, from one metre, a couple centimetres, or 5 metres, or, 100 metres, it's very different. The person who's killed 100 metres away, probably killed in combat, rather than having been executed, so it's very important to know exactly what was the range. I don't know if this also came into the mind of Mr. Seselj, but it's true that through his questions, he seems to be saying that out of the 594 bodies - that's what he says on page 79 - there is obviously some doubts and suspicion as to the range that these people were shot at. I believe this is relevant. Sometimes it seems that there are autopsies that are made without determination of the range.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all my notes were made during the examination-in-chief and the questioning of the Judges. All my associations came on the basis of your questions. I am carefully monitoring and noting down your questions, and I would like this witness to respond to these questions to see if he's a competent expert witness or not. So far, I must say that I'm quite satisfied with his replies, even though you are disrupting me all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that the Judge or the Prosecution during the examination-in-chief have ever asked the witness anything about 15 -- 94 bodies in Srebrenica or something of this, so I don't see any association with the question put by the witness or by the Prosecution, by the Judge, and you asked a lot of questions, but concerning the bodies in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the question was not put, that's true, but there is a series of questions of technical matter that can be put to the witness for Zvornik. And this is your own witness, you know. He's a Prosecution witness, and he has performed a number of autopsies for Srebrenica and other places, so it seems that he does have a lot of expertise, and maybe there is some technical issues that he can answer on. I mean, it's your witness. Remember, this is a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, is it correct that among the exhumed bodies of the Muslim soldiers, there was a substantial number of soldiers who were killed by Howitzer or cannon shrapnel? I don't know the exact number, but were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These were soldiers who were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the breakthrough near Kasaba, and I think that four graves were found at that locality. And among the corpses, there were corpses of soldiers in whose body fragments of explosives and mines were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it's impossible that somebody would execute prisoners from guns?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, it can be done, but it has not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, it's possible. Since I've read all the transcripts from proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic, I know the case of one Albanian who testified viva voce in public in the courtroom who asserted that the Serb police assassinated or executed him from a heavy machine-gun from a distance of 10 metres, and that four bullets ripped through his shirt, and that he was uninjured, and that in reply to a question how it was that he was uninjured and his shirt was ripped in four places, he replied that God saved him. Do you know about that case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that case, but I know a case in Istok, in prison, when there were about 90-some casualties and 100-plus wounded, and those bodies examined by Spanish experts, they said that in 23 bodies, no injuries were found. This was the external examination of the bodies. Then I wrote that these were blast wounds because of the impact, which creates injuries in internal organs, from projectiles that were fired during the NATO aggression. They tried to dispute that, and they said that these members of the Serbian police were actually tying up those Albanians and then threw bombs. I said that then this would be evident and these would not be blast injuries then, because when you have a hand-grenade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, it's time for the break. We will resume in 20 minutes. I hope there will be no objection raised, and I hope that you can finish the hour we have left for your cross-examination. The Prosecutor told us that he needed 15 minutes to talk about something else, so we might run a little bit overboard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Behind schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have 45 minutes left. We will continue 'til 1.15, and that's just 45 minutes. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, did you also come across the fact that some of these international experts in forensic medicine quite arbitrarily made assessments on the number of corpses in mass graves that still hadn't been uncovered?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Wright, an anthropologist from Australia, assessed the corpses in mass graves on the basis of a methodology which determines the quantity of minerals in the soil or perhaps ores in the soil. I challenged that because I thought that was no way of determining this. Everybody has its continuity and its volume. Due to putrefaction in time and because the soft tissue disappears, then it becomes smaller. There are only parts of corpses in some mass graves, so this is an arbitrary assessment which makes it impossible to establish the exact number of persons in mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that the question of the cause of death was completely neglected in these exhumations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that there was this inconsistency. For example, when we did this expertise, when I was involved in this expertise, out of the 2.082 mortal remains - I may be getting the number wrong - but I think that about -- there were about 2.700 causes of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean more causes of death than corpses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which shows that this was done arbitrarily; right? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying arbitrarily, but I'm saying in an unacceptable way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that what was totally neglected was searching for the gunpowder remains on the clothing of the Muslim soldiers who got killed, and these gunpowder remains, if any, would indicate that they were fired at a close range, at short range, and if there is no gunpowder, that would mean that the bullet had been fired from afar; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'd like to clarify this. In forensic medicine, in Serbia, in the former Yugoslavia, quite simply, the firing of projectiles was that they were fired from an absolute close range, which means that the barrel of the weapon is only 5 to 10 millimetres away from clothing or from the body. Relative distance is 10 millimetres to 60 centimetres for short-barrelled weapons and up to one and a half metres, long-barrelled weapons. Beyond that distance, the wounds are inflicted from a faraway distance. On the basis of this, gunpowder can be found. There may be metal particles, too, that are contained once there is an explosion. However, it is irrelevant in this concrete situation. The way in which they worked and the time involved meant that that circumstance had to be investigated too. We did not have any information about that particular matter. When we worked, I spoke about the specific situation in which we carried out the autopsies of Muslims in Zvornik and other corpses in the war-afflicted areas at the time of combat operations. These are -- this is the kind of expertise in exhumation that is conducted in peacetime, which means that gunpowder traces are looked at or searched for on the body of the person involved or the clothing. In this case, this wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know the AK-47, the so-called Kalashnikov, which used to be a standard Yugoslav rifle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If one fires at a victim, at what distance can one find gunpowder on the clothing of the victim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that rifle has a flamethrower, but up to one metre away one can find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, not every rifle has this fire?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not every one does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that one of these renowned international experts by the name of Don Clark claimed that he had established that some persons were buried alive in some of these mass graves? Did you come across such assertions that he made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it possible at all to establish, after all that time, that some person was buried alive in a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the case of bodies that are highly putrid or without skeletisation, this kind of a claim is practically impossible to prove. As for fresh corpses that were buried a few days before the exhumation, it is possible to prove that, and of course it depends on the state of the corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After a year or two or three, it is no longer possible; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were mortal remains that were exhumed, I think, a few years later, so in that situation no such findings could have been made without having witness statements, that is to say, of persons who may have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you read all of these reports, is it not true that this John Clark regularly speaks of models of killing, without going into possible investigations as to whether some wounds could have been inflicted in fighting, in combat, or is he speaking as if it were reliable that these victims had been executed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the reports that I looked at, there was no expertise pertaining to such findings as to whether the persons lost their lives in combat or in some other way, I mean, or whether there were executions. There was an explicit analysis for every case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that after the liberation of Srebrenica, that a large group of Muslim soldiers tried to reach Tuzla on foot?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that this large group, consisting of several thousand persons, directly clashed with the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not have this information. I know that most of these people crossed the territory under Serb control and reached Kladanj. Maybe parts of these units clashed with the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ah-hah. To the best of my knowledge, there was fierce fighting there, and at one moment even the Zvornik Brigade was in danger, and then these Muslims did manage to break through, but many of them lost their lives in these clashes. Also, quite a few Serb soldiers were killed. You haven't heard of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I carried out autopsies of the bodies of some of the soldiers who got killed in the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the clashes with the Muslims who were trying to get through to Tuzla; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do for my purposes. Is it correct that on some exhumed bodies, there were traces of fire on the clothing or on the bones which could indicate that these bodies were taken out of buildings that were on fire?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that may have been the case, but I wrote this a long time ago, and this happened a long time ago. I'm not sure. I think so. It seems that way. It seems that that is written in some of the findings, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that these international experts gave arbitrary assessments of the age of the exhumed persons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did object to the findings of the Peruvian Barobar, and I had most of my objections in relation to what he said. He concluded that a person would be between the age of 17 and 60. That is an objection that was written, and I was present. This was during the trial of General Krstic. I was there in the courtroom, and we were putting questions like that to him. But, yes, there were such estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of some Kitchener, also an international specialist in forensic medicine, who allegedly took part in this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. Well, perhaps, but I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, according to my information, he personally instructed other experts as to how to describe causes of death. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what's written in those papers that were compiled, because there was an objection vis a vis this Kitchener.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Experts complained; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: They complained about this Kitchener who gave some arbitrary information. Also, they complained about him; namely, that part of the clothing that was exhumed was thrown away by him. He just decided to throw it away. And I think that the Tribunal has these complaints lodged by experts, one, two, or three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of William Haglund?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have also heard of Dorothy Gallagher?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Haglund, yes, and I was with him in the courtroom, because I challenged his assertion that only on the basis of bones could one establish when the bone injuries were inflicted. Without soft tissue, I don't know, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information, Dorothy Gallagher, who is also an international expert, made a statement in which she stated that William Haglund was replacing parts of bodies of the persons who were found, or rather the bodily remains that were found.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that statement. I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is a statement made by her. And according to my reliable information, The Hague OTP has that statement. All right. Now, have you heard of David del Pino?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you hear that from the 14th until the 19th of November, 1997, in San Antonio, there was a council of anthropologists and pathologists involved in forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, there was something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to what I have learned, David del Pino made a statement there in writing that this Haglund, William Haglund, asked to have the clothes of the exhumed corpses thrown away. Have you heard something about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that this has to do with Haglund that -- well, I have heard of that. I mentioned that in my previous answer two minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That he was throwing clothes away?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that clothes were thrown away at his discretion. That's probably it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about the replacing of bodily parts? You didn't hear that on purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's contained in Dorothy Gallagher's statement. Do you know that the executive of this council of anthropologists issued a public statement, a public document, in relation to their findings concerning these exhumations of the alleged victims of liquidations after the liberation of Srebrenica? I always have to add that I am not questioning the fact that a number of prisoners were executed, about 1.000, 1.200. I'm not justifying that crime at all, but I'm fighting with all my might against those who would like to exaggerate it many-fold. Do you understand what I'm saying? Have you heard of this public document of theirs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When I carried out my expertise when as a Defence expert when I worked on this, I established that there was this one document of this nature in the material, and it's accessible in the documentation of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that in item 9 of this document, it says that these reports of international forensic medicine experts contain too much subjectivity and too little objectivity and post-mortem examinations of corpses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be specific that that is what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was reading that report, and I read paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've read the report, too, but I cannot recall all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that this report also says that anthropological and pathological investigations were not synchronised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in this report, it says that excessive interference of the media is allowed in the exhumations that were carried out, and that then the experts succumbed to media pressure?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Someone should have told you to read this report before coming here. You did not expect questions like this; you expected questions that were completely different?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I expected what had been announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that this report says that all parties concerned were not allowed to attend at the exhumation of mass graves and that had to be done in accordance with Article 90 of the Additional Protocols to the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For example, the representatives of the Republika Srpska were not allowed to attend during some exhumations of mass graves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that was in the beginning that they were not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Later on, sometimes it was allowed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, it was allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were minister in the last government of the state community of Serbian Montenegro; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At the time when you were minister, the proceedings were still underway according to the alleged complaint of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It wasn't really all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was only the authorities in Sarajevo, but this took place before the International Court of Justice because of allegations of genocide; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Throughout that time, you were a federal minister?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was minister for a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that at the proposal of Vuk Draskovic, Minister of Foreign Affairs, the main representative of Serbia and Montenegro before the International Court of Justice was retired Professor Radoslav Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before him, it was Tibor Validi [phoen], a reputed professional; do you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you agree that Radoslav Stojanovic is no expert whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say, because I know the man only superficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I know him well, and I can say that with certainty. Do you know that under his leadership, the representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, before the International Court of Justice, did not challenge at all that a genocide had occurred in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Federal Government discuss this report of this group of lawyers that represented our state?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Not in my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
