utterances.text: So they could all act -- they could act entirely as they wished?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say, but this was not discussed by the ministerial council at its sessions. That was not a subject of discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Never while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Never while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you believe that this is scandalous, that this was never on the agenda of the ministerial council?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: A lot of scandalous things happened, but I don't want to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Radoslav Stojanovic, as the official representative of our state, did not challenge the figure of 7 to 8.000 allegedly executed Muslim prisoners of war in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He only challenged that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was involved in that, and then the International Court of Justice adjudicated the matter, stating the genocide had happened, but that Serbia was not involved, but was only guilty of not having prevented genocide. Do you know that roughly that was the final judgement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Obviously, it is an entirely false judgement. Do you see that in accordance with the International Convention on Genocide - you should know that as a pathologist and also as a forensic medical expert according to the International Convention on Genocide, what is established is a precise definition of genocide.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot quote it verbatim, but its core is an attempt to destroy or entirely destroy an entire national group or a considerable part of that national group; did I put it right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know that better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. So a protected group, according to the Convention on Genocide, could be all the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the first thing, let me tell you that the translation is lagging behind, and we are receiving the translation a bit after what you say. But I would like to know exactly what is the relevance of your line of questioning? What's the relevance regarding the credibility of the witness? As far as substance is concerned, this has nothing to do with his expert report. You're saying, okay, that you're going through this line of questions to assess the credibility of the witness, but I really don't see your point. Could you please tell us what your point is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Lattanzi, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... questions on the decision of the International Court of Justice, questions on the fact that the International Court of Justice made a number of rulings. I really don't see -- I don't even think that the physician really can understand the ins and outs of these decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to try to answer you in detail, Madame Lattanzi. You saw yesterday how thoroughly I destroyed the testimony of the protected witness. I'm not going to mention his name. I asked him about his father, mother, his first, second, third wife, his children, and in the end, I thoroughly dismantled the evidence. I'm not asking this witness anything from his private life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's up to the Trial Chamber to assess that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are making assessments, but at the end of my cross-examination this witness happened to be the Minister of Defence during a key period. I'm probing his credibility, also on the basis if he ever asked the question at a government meeting of what is being done before the International Court of Justice or what is being done before this Tribunal in The Hague. This is just a quickly-put-together indictment of General Krstic, where it was established that there was no genocide, and then the ICJ takes that as a fact and nobody disputes that it ever happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this has nothing to do with the credibility of the witness. You can continue whichever way you like, but the Judges will take a position on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The presiding judge, I have no problem with taking a position on this. You are, through this witness, criticising the decisions -- the rulings of the ICJ and the fact that this witness was a member of his government at the time. He's only come here to discuss exhumations. I have tried to understand how this can be connected in any way to the ICJ. There's a very tenuous connection. In the ruling of the ICJ, mention is made of destruction of mosques in Mostar, which is something this Tribunal has been seized of also, so there is a connection. But between that and putting questions of such a nature to this witness, who is no legal expert, and he has said that his government does not discuss that, so it would be better if you left it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's relevant. Why was the testimony of that witness relevant who was examined in chief yesterday. You saw that it was not relevant in any way. You saw from the beginning to the end that it was false. I'm not going to mention his name, so I'm not violating anything here. Remarks about relevance are only being addressed to me and never to the Prosecutor. The concept of my Defence is to prove that a large international conspiracy was formed against the Serbian people and that the United States, NATO, European Union, The Hague Tribunal, the International Court of Justice, are all participants in that conspiracy. That will be the topic of my closing statement. Now, I'm gathering information through the cross-examination with which I'm going to support my assertions in my closing statement. I'm sorry that my questions are not in accordance with what you would wish them to be, but I am taking the risk of a bad cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, when you say The Hague Tribunal, anyway, we are not part of a conspiracy, it's good for you to know that. Also, you have 20 minutes left. Try and use your time in your best interest. All the rest you've mentioned already. If you like, I could talk about everything you have said, but use this witness, while he's here, in your best interests.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I know best, I think, what is useful to me. There is no Judge or Prosecutor who could estimate that or assess that better than I could. But at least have the patience sometimes to listen to my cross-examination to the end and then say whether it was of use to me or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now I have forgotten something. Sometimes I have the impression that all these constant interventions of yours serve to make me lose my concentration. All right, I have remembered the evidence. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, are you -- is it clear to you here that this way the genocide -- the judgement on genocide was constructed is based on falsities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't read the judgement all the way through, but my report which I submitted was submitted wholly, as I was told by this session of the Trial Chamber. I really couldn't speak about the particulars of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. What I began to talk about when I was interrupted, by definition of the International Convention on Genocide, a protected group in this case, that could be all of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as such. There were about 2.8 -- 2.180.000, so this is not a significant number, is it? I mean, even if there was 7.000 that we're talking about, it's not even a significant percentage of that total number. So here in this Tribunal, a substitution is being made. Instead of a protected group, pursuant to the Genocide Convention, they are dealing with the protected zone of the United Nations, that is, Srebrenica, and in this substitution they are trying to make it seem as if genocide really did take place. Now, since you did study the documents on these exhumations, I assume that you are familiar with the process of identification of the exhumed persons.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was conducting the autopsies, only 40 bodies were identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that among those exhumed and identified - I don't know if there are 2.300 of them or 3.300 of them - I don't know the exact number - put, anyway, that among them there are people who lived in Zvornik, Bratunac, Vlasenica, even Rogatica, not only in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that particular piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I know about it. Well, perhaps I went into this matter in much more detail. So all the victims are put together, victims of combat -- of course, they are victims, but primarily victims are those who are liquidated. So from different parts of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, that combat at one point concentrated in Srebrenica are then used to declare that genocide was committed against Muslims in Srebrenica. Isn't it true that many of these people were actually from different municipalities, even distant municipalities; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, but at the time when I worked and analysed that material, only 45 bodies out of 2.082 mortal remains were identified, and all of those who were identified were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this question does have some relevance. We have been seized of Zvornik, and there were a lot of victims. This could be a second Srebrenica. I believe that some of the victims in Zvornik have never been found again. Is it technically possible that these victims in Zvornik be discovered in the Srebrenica pits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technically, yes, it is possible to find mass graves in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which would mean that when it comes to assessing Srebrenica, a number of regions would have to be included in the calculations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Theoretically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that during the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the NATO air force used warheads with depleted uranium in the area of Kosovo and Metohija; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: What I dealt with in a bit of detail was depleted uranium in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I know that it was used in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about other parts of Serbia; was such ammunition used?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Such ammunition was used near Vranje, and we cleared the terrain there. Then Orahovac is in Kosovo, but I know for sure that in the area around Vranje and then in Montenegro, on that island, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that in Republika Srpska -- you know that in Republika Srpska, the most characteristic case of using ammunition was depleted uranium was in Hadzici, while Hadzici was still in Serb hands; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the technical centre for armed vehicles was in Hadzici, and in that area a lot of projectiles with such ammunition were fired. After that part of the territory was handed over to the Muslims, 3.500 from those areas moved to Bratunac from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Serbs from there moved to Bratunac. And the last figure that I am aware of is one and a half thousand persons who died of malignant and other diseases. That is why we tried to organise a study on causing consequence between this ammunition and these diseases and causes of death among these persons who died. Since a large number of these people were dying, it was a very large percentage in relation to the persons that had lived in Bratunac before that. There was this characteristic case that we saw where we were not aware of some things, so, for example, Sladjana Sarenac, a girl who was eight or nine years old, she was playing in that crater that had been made by a NATO bomb, and in time her nails fell off, her fingernails and toenails. She got chronic bronchitis, epilepsy, and other diseases, and we linked that to that ammunition. However, later on it turned out that in the gunpowder, there was flourine instead of hydrogen, and therefore it creates an acid, and parts of the human body that get in touch with that acid are affected by irreversible changes. Parts of the body simply fall off. That was the effect of that bombing on that particular person. There is an entire cemetery with the bodily remains of these people in Bratunac. Jancic directed the film, and I know of entire families that died of malignant diseases as an effect of the use of that ammunition. At least that's my opinion. And it didn't happen immediately after the shelling, but a few years afterwards. That's when these illnesses started manifesting themselves in a special way. At that moment, we did not have the right kind of methodology or, rather, we didn't have the apparatus to prove a direct link between that ammunition and the diseases involved. A year later, there were -- the changes on the chromosomes could not be noted, so that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you know that I am rather liberal when it comes to letting you put your questions, but I don't understand what the relevance is here in the Zvornik and Vukovar cases. What is the relevance of this, so many years later, other than you want to claim that NATO bombs caused a lot of damage? But that's been said already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am trying to show what kind of criminals the Serb people had to deal with. And now I'm not referring to criminals from the ranks of the Muslims, the Croats, or the Albanians; I'm referring to the criminal NATO alliance and all of those who took part in the attack against our country. That's what I'm referring to. When I show you what kind of criminals we had to deal with, at least for me that is a slight mitigating circumstance, finally. Right? No, no, it's not a mitigating circumstance for me? All right, there you go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, assuming that what you're saying is founded, this bombing occurred after what you are charged with. These periods do not match. You are using this as a forum to address a well-known topic. We have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not complaining about those ten minutes. That's exactly the amount of time that I'm going to use, the time that I have left, although according to my estimate I have at least 11 or 12 minutes left. So we are going back to the time that is relevant in my indictment, but I am not sure that somebody explained to this expert what is the time relevant for my indictment. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1991, do you know, on the basis of the exhumations that you carried out of Serb soldiers, that is, regardless of whether they were JNA soldiers doing their regular military service, or reservists, or volunteers, or Territorials, do you know that many of them were killed by the Croat hand from weapons that use small-calibre ammunition; for example, sniper rifles or automatic rifles made in Singapore, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, the only mass grave that was dealt with was, well, Vukovar and Siroka Kula near Gospic. However, we did have some injuries caused by projectiles. The entry wound could not be seen, but the exit wound was very big, enormous. Very soon, ballistic experts indicated to us that this was a projectile of the 5.56 calibre - I think that's what it was - that had a terribly destructive effect. Practically, a person that would be hit in the chest or in the abdominal region could not survive because of massive destruction of internal organs, because of the velocity of the projectile movement, so there was -- there were very serious injuries resulting in death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I assume that as a specialist in forensic medicine, you know that this is a banned ammunition from military use.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what they said, and also depleted uranium. Some were trying to persuade us that this was allowed. However, we had been told that it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of my own experience, I will tell you what my knowledge is; not from my personal experience, but what I saw with my very own eyes. So you tell me whether that is correct or not. For example, when a bullet from a small-calibre sniper hits a man in the head, half of his skull can be blown off. And when he's hit in the chest, not only because of the velocity, but also because of the size of the bullet, the bullet does not take a straight line, but it wanders through the body, destroying many organs; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Projectiles from a small-calibre rifle, depending on the angle in which they enter the head or the part of the head that is hit, depending on where the entry wound is and where the exit wound is, it created, yes, wounds, as you had quoted, that would blow off half of the skull, and also in the body, in cavities, destroying soft tissue of different organs and of blood vessels, soft tissues, and they destroy bones. And then these secondary parts of bones would also inflict serious injuries. There were all sorts of things that are in this documentation that is in possession of the Military Medical Academy. There are many such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You said that at one moment that only JNA members and Arkan's men could be distinguished from other people on the Serb side; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not bringing that into question as far as Arkan's men were concerned. They all had special insignia and often they wore black caps with only small slits for the eyes. However, do you know that as far back as in 1991, many JNA soldiers removed the red star from their caps and put the Serb national insignia on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case, even among some of the highest officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that volunteers of the Serb Radical Party got all their equipment only from JNA warehouses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: What was written and said was that they got it from the military facilities in Bubanj Potok. That is what I know, on the basis of what was written. I personally was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said here that all volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were buried at the expense of the JNA or, rather, of the VMA, or any other organ, I don't know exactly, and you said that first of all the autopsy would be carried out at the VMA and then they would be transported to the burial site. Do you also know that there were guards of honour that fired salutes of honour during the funeral?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was the JNA, the General Staff, or the Ministry of Defence that covered the expenses. As for the units for honour, that fired salutes of honour, were regular units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that practically all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were in JNA units until the 19th of May, 1992, while the JNA was still involved in the conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say. I can only say that in terms of what I did and the cooperation I had with Vojvoda Drazilovic and whoever else, I can only speak about that. I cannot speak of other things that happened out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned here your stay in Vukovar immediately after the liberation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 19th and 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the commander of the city when you came to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to Vukovar the first time, it was the representatives of the military police who escorted us, and the investigating judge was there, too. But the second time I came, I reported to General Mrksic's staff. At that time, he was a colonel. And we were met there by the Chief of Staff, Colonel Panic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: That was when we arrived in Vukovar to process the dead bodies. It was on the 19th or the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking about after the liberation of Vukovar, when the Guards Brigade had already withdrawn. They left on the 23rd of November?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: They left on the 23rd, but we arrived on the 19th, 20th, and then we stayed in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Until mid-December, as far as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Until you completed your work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until we completed our work. Later on, the commander of town was Vojnovic, I think it was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was commander, but I know he was the commander of the town, and I think that it was close to the railway station or some railway facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since I don't have any time left, just two or three questions, so let me try to cut things short. You said, and I was surprised by that, that you were not provided security by the military, but by the Territorial Defence. Isn't it clear to you that it was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic who had, under his command, the Territorial Defence too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. When we started looking for the corpses --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade was there after the 23rd of November.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: But after that, after these first few days while we were looking for a place where we would process these corpses, it was these people. After that, we did not have any security. All the teams went around without any security whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No security was needed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody impeded your work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody impeded my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't even know about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't. We would have exhumed had we known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there were those who didn't want to tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just briefly on the question of Zvornik, since I will be interrupted shortly: In view of the fact that you went to Zvornik twice on the 30th of April and the 5th of May, 1992, it is my impression that the JNA tried to properly do the whole procedure relating to the victims of the conflict, both from the opposing side and to establish the cause of death of everybody according to the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And this could have taken until the 19th of May, at the latest, when the army withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct? You know that -- I assume that the bulk of the victims of various liquidations, killings, tortures, and so on occurred in June 1992, when the JNA was no longer there. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the media, not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Judging by everything when you were performing the autopsies, the majority of the Muslim fighters that were killed were killed in combat. I'm not ruling out the possibility, and we did have witnesses here who talked about some 20 victims -- or civilians killed in Zvornik, and it is known who killed them, but this is not really all that important for this particular discussion of ours here now. But evidently all the bodies found at Kula Grad were bodies of those killed in combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were killed in combat, but I said that there were two bodies, one of them had a stab wound as the only injury in the left side of the chest, in the heart area, and there was one case with two cuts on the right side of the neck and the right side of the face. These people most probably were killed by another person. I don't know if this was in combat or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This statement that you gave in 2003, I looked at it, and I can see something here that is quite strange. The conversation with you was conducted on the 8th of July, 2003, and it was read back to you on the 1st of October, 2003. Why this passage of time between the conversation and the actual statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke many times with people from The Hague Tribunal in my capacity as a committee member or in other capacities, so when I provided my first statement, where I said a number of things, there were some objections or remarks to my findings and opinions, and additional explanations were required about the cause of death and other causes. So they came to the VMA on a number of occasions. This is definitely correct, but I really cannot give you an explanation why it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your first statement amounted to some 70 pages?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the autopsies of Serbian victims are discussed in various locations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Fakovici, Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These are civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly civilian victims with some members of the AVRS, but let's say Miladin Aseric, whose head was cut off, and Trisa who was strangled with some piece of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this is a fact, that The Hague Tribunal never showed any inclination to use that first statement of yours in any proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, there was talk about me coming to testify in the Nasir Oric case, but his Defence accepted my report in its entirety, so I was finally never summoned to come to the trial to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you've used up your full hour, so we will put a stop to this now. Mr. Witness, thank you for coming here. I wish you a safe return home. I'll ask the usher to please escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now give the floor to Mr. Mundis. I believe he has something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am aware of the time, and I will move as quickly as I possibly can, but of course allowing the interpreters to keep up with me. Your Honours, following the hearing of the first witness that we heard this week, the Prosecution makes this urgent oral application for the immediate adjournment of these proceedings, in light of clear evidence that the proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should this be in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe that I can make some introductory remarks in open session. We believe, Your Honours, that there is clear evidence that the proceedings are being interfered with and the integrity of the proceedings is being compromised. Of course, it's fully within the Trial Chamber's duties and obligations to protect the integrity of the proceedings and to ensure that the trial is fair both to the accused, but also to the Prosecution. We submit that the Trial Chamber has an obligation to suspend the proceedings when faced with clear and convincing evidence that going forward will compromise the integrity and fairness of the proceedings. Moreover, as the Statute makes clear, the Chamber has an obligation to ensure the safety and security of victims and witnesses, and that the victims and witnesses are treated with dignity and respect. And, Your Honours, at this point I would ask to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving to closed session, I have something to add. Mr. Seselj, just a minute. I would like to say something. I wanted to say something to Mr. Mundis. You only have about 18 hours left to present your case, and now you're asking about a suspension of these proceedings because, allegedly, witnesses would be jeopardising the integrity of this Tribunal because of pressure exerted on them. If witnesses are pressure and if pressure is exerted on the witnesses, this will be established at one point in time. However, these witnesses are coming here to the hearings. In the hearings, they're in your hands. You're the Prosecutor, you're asking the questions, and in doing so you can ask all the questions you want to the witnesses, and then the accused will do the cross-examination. But the Judges do their job. The Judges have elements to assess the situation, and I can tell you that they check everything that the witnesses say. Let's not confuse things. The integrity of the Tribunal is make sure that the trial is speedy and that there is a judgement, and that we don't play cat-and-mouse all the time. But when a witness actually comes, be it a Court witness, a Defence witness or a Prosecution witness, he can come, he can say the truth, he can lie - I don't know anything about it - but he is screened through the Prosecution's question, through the Defence's question, and through the questions put to him or her by the Judges, and the Judges can find out and can recognise whether the witness is telling the truth or whether he's lying. But independently of the witnesses, there are also documents, and documents don't usually lie. We are only 18 hours from the closing of your case, and you're coming back to this problem with the suspension, based on what happened yesterday, what might have happened yesterday. I'm saying what allegedly happened yesterday, because we need to look into what actually happened yesterday. But yesterday, we had a witness here who answered according to the statement that he had made in 2003 or 2000 -- I can't remember. And all witnesses who made their statements when nothing was happening in 2003 and 2004 did come, and if they don't show up, the Trial Chamber - and I told you clearly - the Trial Chamber will, anyway, admit these statements. But I believe that the trial must absolutely continue. I believe you now want to move to closed session, so Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, please. I have a right to reply to the public part of Mr. Mundis's statement, and then you can move to private session. Gentlemen Judges, you were able to see with your own eyes yesterday and hear with your own ears with what ease I demolished the entire testimony of the Prosecution witness. I am asking you then: What would be my interest to intimidate such a witness in any way? What interest of mine would that be? I am lucky to have a witness like that come as a witness of the Prosecution. What would I have done with him had he happened by chance to be a witness for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would ask that this be moved into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
